weeks: Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb

questions.stem: A student asks what gives normal synovial fluid its thick, viscous quality when it is aspirated from a healthy knee during an arthrocentesis teaching session. Which component is chiefly responsible for synovial fluid viscosity?
questions.explain: Hyaluronate (with lubricin), added by type B synoviocytes to a plasma ultrafiltrate, makes fluid viscous. Type II collagen is a solid of cartilage matrix; leukocytes and immunoglobulins are immune components, and when leukocytes rise in inflammation viscosity actually falls.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic hand pain has X-rays reviewed. The radiologist is asked which single finding would point to an inflammatory arthritis rather than osteoarthritis. Which radiographic change best supports inflammatory arthritis?
questions.explain: Erosions (marginal, at the bare area where synovium doubles over) reflect inflammatory pannus destroying bone. Osteophytes, subchondral cysts and focal narrowing are OA changes: OA remodels and lays down bone; RA destroys it and never makes osteophytes.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old teacher has 4 months of hand pain. Which additional history feature would most strongly suggest an inflammatory rather than mechanical cause, according to the approach taught in CBL and the joint-pain module?
options: Pain that builds through the day and is worst at bedtime
Stiffness lasting about 90 minutes each morning that eases with use
Pain that settles after a few minutes of rest
questions.explain: Prolonged morning stiffness that improves with activity is the hallmark of inflammation (the CBL tutor's cut-off was >1 hour). End-of-day pain, crepitus and relief with rest are mechanical/OA features. Inflammatory pain also wakes patients at 3–6 am rather than stopping them getting to sleep.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old has a swollen right elbow for 5 days. He is afebrile and otherwise well. Aspirated fluid is turbid with a WBC of 28,000 ×10<sup>6</sup>/L; Gram stain is pending. How is this fluid best classified at this point?
questions.explain: WBC >2,000 is inflammatory; septic fluid is typically >50,000 with 80–90% PMNs, but that is a guideline only. 28,000 without systemic features is best called inflammatory; culture still decides infection. Non-inflammatory is <2,000.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old mother of a toddler in daycare has 3 weeks of symmetric swelling of MCPs, PIPs and wrists with 1 h of morning stiffness. RF is weakly positive. What single feature would most help distinguish her likely diagnosis from early RA?
options: Resolution of symptoms within about 2 months
questions.explain: This is classic parvovirus B19 arthritis: an RA-like symmetric small-joint polyarthritis in a parent of a daycare child. It is self-limited over ~6–8 weeks, which is why the RA criteria reward ≥6 weeks' duration and why >3 months effectively excludes parvovirus. Symmetry, wrists and even RF don't separate them.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has 2 months of a swollen left knee and right ankle, a sausage-shaped second toe and heel pain at the Achilles insertion. No back pain. Spine and SI joints are normal on exam. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis with dactylitis and enthesitis = peripheral SpA. AS needs axial/SI involvement; RA is symmetric small-joint; DGI is migratory with tenosynovitis and pustules in an acutely unwell patient.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old develops an asymmetric arthritis of one knee and ankle, conjunctivitis and dysuria two weeks after a bout of bloody diarrhea from a barbecue. Joint aspiration shows inflammatory fluid with a negative culture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Reactive arthritis: asymmetric oligoarthritis 1–3 weeks (PW03; 1–4 in the ISAL) after a GI or GU infection, with conjunctivitis, urethritis and mucosal ulcers. The joint is sterile (immune-mediated). Enteropathic arthritis tracks chronic IBD activity.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing inflammatory back pain and bilateral sacroiliitis presents with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision. Which extra-articular manifestation is most characteristic of this family of arthritis?
questions.explain: Iritis/uveitis is the eye manifestation of the seronegative spondyloarthritides (especially AS). Scleritis and episcleritis are the seropositive (RA) eye lesions, and sicca points to Sjögren's or RA.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with hepatitis C develops symmetric polyarthritis of small and large joints over 2 months. You have moderate pre-test suspicion for RA. Which test would best confirm RA with the fewest false positives in this patient?
questions.explain: Anti-CCP has similar sensitivity to RF (~68%) but ~95% specificity. RF is a poor choice here: hepatitis C (and cryoglobulinemia, SBE, Sjögren's) commonly cause a positive RF. CRP is non-specific; ENA is for CTDs.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman who works as a typist has 2 years of pain in both thumb bases, PIPs and knees with typing, 10 minutes of morning stiffness, bony DIP enlargement and no effusions. A prior RF was 178 IU (N<12). ESR is 25. What is the best interpretation?
options: Osteoarthritis; the RF is likely a false positive
questions.explain: Mechanical pain, brief stiffness, CMC/PIP/DIP bony changes and no synovitis = OA. Pre-test probability for RA was low, so a positive RF mostly reflects a false positive. Her ESR is normal: ULN = (46 + 10)/2 = 28.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with known SLE presents with fatigue, arthralgia, a new oral ulcer and mild pedal edema. You suspect a flare. Which investigation is most important to include in the initial workup?
questions.explain: The priority is detecting lupus nephritis: no exam maneuver finds glomerulonephritis, and pedal edema raises concern. ANA won't change management once SLE is diagnosed; ESR will be high in a flare anyway. Anti-dsDNA and C3/C4 track activity, but Cr + UA define organ damage.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with fatigue and diffuse aches but no rash, synovitis, cytopenia or proteinuria has an ANA of 1:160 on a screening panel ordered by a walk-in clinic. Which statement best guides your next step?
options: About 5% of healthy people have ANA ≥1:160, so without clinical features this is probably not SARD
She needs anti-dsDNA and complement urgently
A positive ANA means she will develop lupus within 5 years
questions.explain: ANA is sensitive but not specific: ~5% of normal people are positive at 1:160 (20–30% at 1:40), more with female sex and age. It should only be ordered at moderate pre-test probability. Without features she needs symptom screening and reassurance, not reflex sub-serologies.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has Raynaud's with digital pitting scars, sclerodactyly limited to her fingers and face, heartburn, dysphagia and facial telangiectasias. Which autoantibody is most likely to be positive?
questions.explain: This is limited cutaneous SSc (CREST): Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia, with prominent vasculopathy: anti-centromere. Anti-Scl-70 = diffuse SSc (fibrosis, ILD); Jo-1 = anti-synthetase myositis; Sm = SLE.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with diabetes and a right knee replacement has 2 days of a hot, swollen knee and a temperature of 38.6°C. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start oral cephalexin and review in 1 week
Aspirate the joint and draw blood cultures, then start empiric IV antibiotics
questions.explain: Fever + hot joint + prosthesis + diabetes = septic until proven otherwise. Culture first (synovial Gram stain/culture, cell count, crystals + blood cultures), then empiric IV antibiotics covering S. aureus, tailored to cultures, plus source control. Oral antibiotics are undertreatment; steroid injection into an infected joint is dangerous.

questions.stem: An adult with no risk factors for sexually transmitted infection develops septic arthritis of the knee after a skin infection on the leg. Which organism should empiric antibiotic therapy be chosen primarily to cover?
questions.explain: S. aureus is the most common cause of adult septic arthritis (gram-positive cocci 75–80%), usually by hematogenous spread from skin, lung, urine or endocarditis. Add gram-negative/strep cover in the elderly or immunocompromised and think gonococcus in the sexually active.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has 4 days of fever, pain moving from wrist to ankle, tenderness along the dorsal hand tendons and a few small hemorrhagic pustules on the fingers and feet. What additional testing is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Cultures of the oropharynx, urethra/cervix and rectum plus blood cultures
questions.explain: Migratory arthritis + tenosynovitis + pustules on the limbs = disseminated gonococcal infection. Culture the entry sites (oropharynx, urethra/cervix/vagina, rectum) and blood, and aspirate any effusion. Incidence is rising in young adults.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old returns from a work trip with a fever of 38.5°C and an acutely hot, exquisitely tender left ankle. Which exam finding would make joint aspiration most clearly indicated?
options: Symmetric swelling of the wrists and elbows
No inflammation in any other joint
questions.explain: An isolated hot joint is a monoarthritis, which must be aspirated to rule out septic arthritis and look for crystals (3 C's). Polyarticular findings shift the differential toward systemic or viral disease; Heberden's nodes are OA.

questions.stem: Two days after a urologic operation, a 70-year-old man develops a hot, swollen left knee. Aspirate: WBC 50,000 ×10<sup>6</sup>/L, Gram stain negative, needle-shaped intracellular crystals that are strongly negatively birefringent. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals = gout; surgery is a classic trigger. CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positive; hydroxyapatite isn't seen on routine microscopy. Still await the culture: crystals and infection can coexist.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old had his first documented gout attack in the knee 2 weeks ago, now resolved. Exam is normal, creatinine normal, urate 510 µmol/L, no tophi or stones. What is the best management now?
options: Monitor for further attacks and give a plan (e.g. colchicine) for any future flare
Keep him on a daily NSAID indefinitely
questions.explain: After a first attack without CKD, very high urate or stones, don't start ULT: monitor and treat future flares early. ULT is for recurrent attacks (≥2/yr), tophi or radiographic damage. Never treat asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Gout is managed in primary care.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman has a 5-day hot, swollen right wrist. Aspirate: WBC 30,000 (88% PMN), rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals, culture negative. X-ray shows linear calcification of the triangular fibrocartilage. What is the best treatment?
questions.explain: Acute pseudogout (CPPD): older patient, wrist, positive crystals, chondrocalcinosis. Treat the inflammation with an NSAID or glucocorticoid (intra-articular works well). Culture is negative, so antibiotics aren't needed. Allopurinol treats urate, not CPPD, and colchicine is less helpful acutely.

questions.stem: A healthy 41-year-old plays tennis on Friday and wakes Sunday with severe right shoulder pain. He cannot actively abduct, but the examiner can move the glenohumeral joint passively with modest discomfort. X-ray shows a periarticular calcific density. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Hydroxyapatite causes acute periarthritis in younger people at the shoulder, hip or first MTP of a young woman. Active movement is too painful but passive movement is preserved (it wouldn't be in a true monoarthritis). Periarticular calcification is visible on X-ray; the crystals aren't seen on routine microscopy.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old with stage 3b CKD and heart failure on furosemide and ramipril develops acute gout of the first MTP. Besides GI bleeding, which NSAID complication most argues for choosing a different drug for his flare?
options: Nephrotoxicity with sodium and potassium retention
questions.explain: NSAIDs block renal prostaglandins → Na/water retention, hyperkalemia, worsening CHF and AKI, especially with ACEi and diuretics. Prefer a glucocorticoid (oral or intra-articular); colchicine is also poorly cleared in renal disease.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has 3 months of progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair, and has given up tennis. She denies joint pain or stiffness. Exam shows symmetric proximal weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Painless proximal weakness = inflammatory myositis (check CK, then MRI, EMG, antibodies, biopsy). PMR causes proximal pain and stiffness without true weakness and needs age ≥50. RA and fibromyalgia don't cause objective weakness.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old lawyer reports fingers that turn white then red in the cold. Which additional history feature would most raise your concern that her Raynaud's is secondary to a systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease?
questions.explain: SARDs are multisystem: Raynaud's plus lung involvement (ILD or pulmonary hypertension) suggests scleroderma or another CTD. Also look for digital pitting, abnormal nailfold capillaries, rash, synovitis and dysphagia. Mechanical knee pain and headaches don't cluster with SARDs.

questions.stem: A patient with a systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease develops palpable purpura on the legs and new proteinuria with red cell casts. Serum C3 and C4 are low. What immune mechanism most likely explains these findings?
questions.explain: Skin vasculitis and glomerulonephritis with low complement = immune-complex deposition. By contrast, immune thrombocytopenia and autoimmune hemolysis are direct autoantibody-mediated, and myositis is largely T-cell driven.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has fatigue, a facial rash, oral ulcers, inflammatory hand pain and pleuritic chest pain with small effusions. Hb 100, WBC 3.2, platelets 110. ANA is positive. Which result would be most specific for SLE?
questions.explain: Anti-Sm (and anti-dsDNA) are highly specific for SLE; low C3/C4 supports active disease. Anti-Ro is also seen in Sjögren's; RF and ESR are non-specific. Her features fit RASH OR PAIN: rash, arthritis, serositis, hematologic, oral ulcers, ANA.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old has 3 weeks of new temporal headache, jaw pain after chewing and shoulder stiffness. This morning she lost vision in the right eye for 10 minutes. ESR 88, platelets 520. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Book a temporal artery biopsy and start steroids once it is positive
IV pulse methylprednisolone now, with urgent ophthalmology and rheumatology
questions.explain: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms is an emergency: 1 g IV methylprednisolone (without visual loss: prednisone 1 mg/kg). Don't delay steroids for the biopsy (the gold standard, which stays positive for a while after starting treatment). Low-dose prednisone is for PMR alone.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has 6 weeks of aching and 90 minutes of morning stiffness in both shoulders and hips, trouble getting out of a chair, and no headache or visual symptoms. ESR 62, CRP 48, RF and anti-CCP negative. Strength is normal when pain allows. Best initial treatment?
questions.explain: PMR: ≥50, shoulder/hip girdle pain and stiffness, high inflammatory markers, negative RF/CCP, no true weakness. Treat with low–medium dose glucocorticoid. Screen for GCA (about 20% of PMR); GCA needs high dose.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old has 2 years of widespread aching in both arms, legs, back and chest, unrefreshing sleep, poor concentration and weight gain. Exam shows diffuse tenderness only; CBC, CK, TSH, ESR and CRP are normal. What is the best first-line management?
options: Education, graded exercise, CBT and sleep strategies
questions.explain: Fibromyalgia (≥3 months, ≥6/9 sites, sleep/fatigue/cognitive symptoms, normal exam and labs). Non-pharmacologic therapy beats drugs; add duloxetine or pregabalin if needed. NSAIDs and opioids are not recommended (opioids may worsen it). Avoid repeated investigation.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old has 2 months of fever, 8 kg weight loss, new foot drop, and palpable purpura on the shins. Which bedside test is most important to do next?
questions.explain: A constitutionally ill patient with multisystem disease (skin, nerve) suggests systemic vasculitis. Palpable purpura = small-vessel disease, so screen the kidney with urinalysis (hematuria, proteinuria), then ANCA and creatinine.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old has 3 months of synovitis in both wrists, MCP2–5, PIP2–5, knees and MTP2–5. RF 200 and anti-CCP 80 (ULN 20 for both); ESR and CRP are normal. What is her 2010 ACR/EULAR classification score?
questions.explain: >10 joints including small = 5; high-positive serology (>3× ULN) = 3; normal ESR and CRP = 0; duration ≥6 weeks = 1. Total 9 (≥6 = definite RA). Remember these are classification (research) criteria, not diagnostic ones.

questions.stem: A patient with seropositive RA asks whether her RF titre should be rechecked every visit to see if methotrexate is working. What is the best response?
options: Yes, a falling RF titre shows disease control
No, RF doesn't track activity, though a high titre predicts a more aggressive course
Yes, but only anti-CCP should be followed
No, because RF becomes negative once RA is controlled
questions.explain: RF and anti-CCP reflect disease course and severity (erosions, extra-articular disease), not current activity, so don't repeat them. Monitor with joint counts, composite scores (DAS28, CDAI), ESR/CRP, function and imaging.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with long-standing seropositive RA develops new hematuria, proteinuria and a rising creatinine. Why should this prompt a search for another diagnosis?
options: RA frequently causes crescentic GN, so none is needed
The kidney is largely spared in RA, so consider lupus, Sjögren's, vasculitis or drug toxicity
Rheumatoid nodules commonly form in the kidney
questions.explain: RA can involve almost any organ (nodules, scleritis, ILD, pleuritis, pericarditis, Felty's) but largely spares the kidney (amyloid and RTA are rare). Renal disease should point you to overlap/lupus, Sjögren's, vasculitis or medication (e.g. NSAIDs).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with RA well controlled on adalimumab for a year presents with 2 days of fever and a single red, hot, swollen right knee. No other joints are active. What is the next most important investigation?
options: Urgent arthrocentesis for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals
Increase the adalimumab dose for a flare
questions.explain: On a TNF inhibitor, a single hot febrile joint with otherwise quiet disease is septic until proven otherwise. Aspirate (add AFB/fungal if at risk; TB reactivation is a real risk), take blood cultures and hold the biologic. Biologics can blunt fever and cell counts. A monoarticular flare is a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with RA was started on methotrexate by her rheumatologist. As her family physician, which toxicity should your routine bloodwork primarily monitor for?
questions.explain: Low-dose methotrexate causes hepatic, GI and hematologic toxicity and oral ulcers; monitor CBC, liver enzymes and creatinine (monthly at first, then every ~3 months). It's given once weekly with daily folic acid except the MTX day, and it is teratogenic: contraception is essential.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with newly diagnosed seropositive RA plans to try for a second child next year. Which disease-modifying approach is most appropriate to start now?
questions.explain: Methotrexate and leflunomide are contraindicated in pregnancy. Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine (and certolizumab among biologics) are compatible; the CBL rheumatologist would use HCQ first-line here. Waiting risks irreversible erosions: RA should be treated within ~3 months.

questions.stem: Before starting a TNF-α inhibitor for refractory RA, which pre-treatment screening is essential?
options: Latent TB screening (with chest X-ray) and hepatitis B serology
questions.explain: Biologics risk reactivation of latent TB and hepatitis B and opportunistic infection. Screen first, update vaccines (no live vaccines once on therapy), and hold the drug for intercurrent infection and surgery. Anti-TNFs also raise non-melanoma skin cancer risk.

questions.stem: A patient on prednisone 20 mg daily is admitted and made NPO. Using standard equivalents, what IV methylprednisolone dose is approximately equivalent?
questions.explain: Prednisone 5 mg = methylprednisolone 4 mg = hydrocortisone 20 mg, so prednisone 20 mg is about methylprednisolone 16 mg (or hydrocortisone 80 mg). 20 mg of prednisone is a medium dose (low ≤15, medium 20–40, high 40–60+).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old falls from a bike and sustains a displaced mid-shaft humeral fracture. On exam he cannot extend his wrist or fingers. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
questions.explain: The radial nerve (with the profunda brachii artery) runs in the radial groove directly on the posterior shaft, so mid-shaft fractures injure it, causing wrist drop. Surgical-neck fractures endanger the axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor); median and ulnar are cushioned by muscle.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old painter has weakness when you resist abduction with the arm at 45° and the thumb pointing down, and pain when you passively forward-flex his internally rotated arm. Which muscle is most likely affected?
questions.explain: The empty-can test isolates supraspinatus (initiates abduction; suprascapular nerve), and Neer's test is positive with subacromial impingement, because its tendon passes under the coracoacromial arch. Infraspinatus/teres minor = resisted ER; subscapularis = resisted IR.

questions.stem: A rugby player lands on the point of his shoulder. X-ray shows the distal clavicle displaced superiorly relative to the acromion, with a normal glenohumeral articulation. Which injury is this, and which joint is involved?
questions.explain: A separated shoulder is disruption of the AC joint (and the coracoclavicular ligament, its main stabilizer); the true shoulder joint is intact. A dislocated shoulder is loss of contact at the glenohumeral joint.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old has numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers at night and thenar weakness, but normal sensation over the thenar eminence of the palm. Why is palmar sensation preserved?
options: The ulnar nerve supplies the whole palm
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The radial nerve supplies the thenar skin
The median nerve lies outside the carpal tunnel
questions.explain: In carpal tunnel syndrome the median nerve is compressed under the flexor retinaculum with the 4 FDS, 4 FDP and FPL tendons. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves proximally and runs over the retinaculum, so palm sensation is spared. A higher median lesion would also numb the palm.

questions.stem: A patient has a deep laceration in the cubital fossa that transects the tendon inserting on the radial tuberosity. Which movement will be most weakened, beyond elbow flexion?
questions.explain: The biceps brachii inserts on the radial tuberosity and is a powerful supinator (with supinator). Because only the radius rotates, muscles attaching to the ulna (brachialis, triceps) can't pronate or supinate. The biceps tendon lies lateral to the brachial artery and median nerve in the fossa.

questions.stem: After a fall on an outstretched hand, a 19-year-old has tenderness in the depression between the EPL and EPB/APL tendons at the dorsolateral wrist. Which bone forms the floor of this region, and which artery crosses it?
questions.explain: The anatomical snuff box floor is the scaphoid and trapezium; the radial artery, cephalic vein and superficial radial nerve cross it. Snuff-box tenderness after a FOOSH = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old reports that the right ring finger catches and sometimes locks in flexion, then snaps straight. There is tenderness and a palpable nodule over the palmar aspect of the MCP joint. Which structure is most likely involved?
questions.explain: Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis) involves a long digital flexor tendon catching at the palmar MCP; the lecture answer is FDS. FPL moves the thumb only; the flexor retinaculum is at the wrist (carpal tunnel); extensors are dorsal.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old has 2 weeks of difficulty walking. When she stands on her right leg, her left pelvis drops. Which finding identifies hip pathology as the source, and which muscles are weak?
options: Trendelenburg sign; right gluteus medius and minimus
questions.explain: A Trendelenburg sign/gait reflects weak hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) on the stance side, so the opposite pelvis drops. In the back exam it tests L5 hip abduction. Steppage gait = foot drop (L5/peroneal).

questions.stem: A 71-year-old has leg-dominant pain that comes on after walking two blocks, forces him to sit or lean forward on a shopping cart to get relief, and fully resolves at rest. SLR is negative. Which mechanical pattern is this?
questions.explain: Intermittent, leg-dominant pain aggravated by extension (walking) and relieved by flexion (sitting) with negative irritative tests = Pattern 4 FR, neurogenic claudication (spinal stenosis). Pattern 3 is constant leg pain with a positive SLR or deficit.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old has lateral shoulder pain only when reaching overhead. Active abduction is painful between 60° and 120°, but passive range is full and much less painful, and there is no warmth or effusion. What does this pattern indicate?
questions.explain: Periarticular disease hurts only in the direction that loads the structure and is much less painful passively. Articular disease hurts through the whole active and passive range, often with stress pain, warmth or effusion (inflammation) or crepitus and limited range (damage).

questions.stem: A 38-year-old has back and buttock pain plus aching behind the thigh. Asked where it's worst, she says 'everywhere, I need it all fixed'. What is the best next question to classify her pain pattern?
options: 'If I could stop only one pain today, which would it be?'
questions.explain: Pattern recognition starts with dominance: back (above the inferior gluteal fold) vs leg. Force a choice empathetically: "If I could only stop one pain, which would it be?" Pain quality doesn't classify the pattern. If she truly can't decide, assume leg-dominant (the worst case).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with back-dominant pain says it 'eases off to almost nothing' when he lies down in the evening, but it never quite disappears. How should his pain be classified, and why does it matter?
options: Intermittent, which rules out red flags
Constant, since 'almost nothing' isn't completely gone, so screen for red flags
Intermittent, so it must be Pattern 2
questions.explain: Ask in two parts: does the pain ever stop, and when it stops is it completely gone? "Nearly/mostly gone" counts as constant. Constant back-dominant pain is Pattern 1 if flexion-aggravated, but it warrants red-flag questions. Only truly intermittent back pain excludes malignancy and infection.

questions.stem: During a straight leg raise at 40°, a patient with back-dominant pain reports that her usual low back pain increases, but she has no leg pain. How should the test be recorded?
options: Positive: nerve root irritation at L5/S1
Negative: only reproduction of the typical leg pain counts
Positive, but only if the pain began below 30°
Equivocal: repeat with the knee bent
questions.explain: A positive SLR reproduces or worsens the typical leg-dominant pain, at any angle. Back pain alone is not positive; it only shows mechanical pain. Keep the other hip and knee flexed to remove hamstring tightness. A back-dominant patient shouldn't have a positive SLR.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old has constant low back pain, worse sitting and bending; the neuro exam is normal. After 10 prone passive extensions his pain is unchanged. Which classification and first management fit best?
options: Pattern 1 PEN: scheduled rest (Z-lie, prone over pillows), then progress toward extension
questions.explain: Back-dominant, flexion-aggravated pain = Pattern 1; no improvement with 10 press-ups = PEN (no directional preference). Start with scheduled rest positions (Z-lie, prone over pillows) and a small lumbar roll, then progress: knees-to-chest → prone over pillows → prone press-ups, then treat as PEP.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old gymnast has intermittent low back pain on back walkovers and standing; it never hurts to bend forward, and touching her toes eases it. Neuro exam normal. What pattern and exercise approach fit?
options: Pattern 2: flexion exercises such as seated slump and step flexion
questions.explain: Pattern 2: back-dominant, always intermittent, never worse with flexion, worse with extension (a facet pattern in gymnasts and overhead workers). Treat with flexion: seated slump stretch and step flexion, plus a pillow between the knees at night. Pain control is usually rapid.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with back pain and bilateral leg paresthesia has a normal SLR, but on exam there are 6 sustained beats of ankle clonus and an extensor plantar response. What does this imply?
options: The mechanical back diagnosis is negated: refer to neurology to work up an upper motor neuron problem
questions.explain: Any UMN finding (spasticity, extensor plantar response, sustained clonus) negates a mechanical low back diagnosis: the lesion is above the cauda equina (cord or brain, e.g. cervical/thoracic myelopathy). 1–2 beats of clonus can be normal; sustained beats aren't. The tutor's framing: it isn't a 911 red flag like cauda equina, but it needs a neurology referral for further testing.

questions.stem: On examining a knee, you sweep up the medial side, then stroke down the lateral side, and no fluid bulges back into the medial fossa. The suprapatellar area is visibly full, and pressing the patella with the pouch compressed gives a clear tap. What does this mean?
options: A large effusion: too much fluid to sweep, detected by ballottement
questions.explain: The bulge sign detects small effusions; a large effusion can't be displaced, so the bulge is absent. Ballottement/patellar tap (compress the suprapatellar pouch, press the patella) detects larger effusions. Prepatellar bursitis is superficial to the patella and spares the joint.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old new mother has pain at the radial side of the wrist when lifting her baby. Pain is reproduced when she tucks her thumb into her fist and you ulnar-deviate the wrist. Which structures are involved?
options: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons (De Quervain's)
questions.explain: A positive Finkelstein's test = De Quervain's tenosynovitis of the APL and EPB tendons (the radial border of the snuff box), from overuse and repetitive wrist movement. Carpal tunnel is tested with Tinel's and Phalen's; CMC OA gives squaring and basal thumb pain.

questions.stem: Examining a painful shoulder, you place the patient's elbow at the side, rotate the forearm outward, then ask her to resist as you push it back toward the abdomen. She is weak and in pain. Which structures are you testing?
questions.explain: Resisting a push back toward neutral from external rotation tests external rotators: infraspinatus and teres minor. Resisted internal rotation tests subscapularis; the empty can tests supraspinatus; Neer's tests impingement.

questions.stem: Which structure is the joint's best defence against bacteria seeded from the bloodstream?
questions.explain: The synovial membrane: it is vascular (so blood-borne bacteria reach it first) and contains the phagocytic Type A synoviocytes. Cartilage is avascular, and normal synovial fluid has too few WBCs/macrophages to protect the joint (SLM06).

questions.stem: A positive c-ANCA with anti-PR3 on ELISA is most associated with which group of diseases?
questions.explain: c-ANCA → anti-PR3; p-ANCA → anti-MPO. Both mark the small-vessel ANCA vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA). Immunofluorescence needs ELISA confirmation (PW05).

questions.stem: A serologic test has 92% sensitivity and 92% specificity. It comes back negative in a patient you think has a 90% chance of the disease. What is the post-test probability?
questions.explain: At high pre-test probability a negative result still leaves about 43%, just as a positive result at 10% pre-test gives only 56%. Only at intermediate pre-test (50% → 92% if positive, 8% if negative) does the test move you decisively (PW04).

questions.stem: Which crystal arthropathy has no preventive (long-term) therapy available, according to the monoarthritis lecture?
options: All three can be prevented with urate-lowering therapy
questions.explain: Gout is prevented with lifestyle and urate-lowering therapy. For CPPD and hydroxyapatite there is nothing available to date; colchicine can be tried for chronic CPPD (Lec01).

questions.stem: Glucocorticoids are the usual initial therapy for most SARDs. Which disease is the exception, and why?
options: Scleroderma, because it is fibrotic and vasculopathic rather than inflammatory
questions.explain: Lec02: in most SARDs, inflammation drives treatment (glucocorticoids, then a steroid-sparing agent), except scleroderma, which is not inflammatory but fibrotic and vasculopathic. Moderate/high-dose steroids are generally avoided in SSc because they raise the risk of scleroderma renal crisis (standard).

questions.stem: Which of the following most increases the risk of gout through reduced renal urate excretion?
questions.explain: About 70% of urate is excreted by the kidney. Risk factors for poor excretion: genetics, metabolic syndrome, renal impairment and drugs such as diuretics (Lec01).

questions.stem: A patient has numbness over the lateral forearm and weak elbow flexion after a penetrating injury to the anterior arm. Which nerve is injured?
questions.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve (lateral cord) pierces coracobrachialis, supplies the anterior arm flexors and ends as the skin supply of the lateral forearm. The ulnar nerve supplies nothing in the arm.

questions.stem: According to the Ortho Back student guide, how is the femoral nerve stretch test performed?
options: Supine, straight leg lifted with the other knee flexed
Prone, knee of the painful leg extended, examiner lifts the leg into hip extension
questions.explain: Passive test: patient prone, knee of the painful leg extended, examiner lifts the leg. Positive = reproduces the typical anterior thigh (L3/4) pain; back pain is common but irrelevant. (The tutor demonstrated a knee-flexed variant.)

cards.prompt: Name the four components a healthy synovial joint depends on and one function of each.
cards.answer: Articular cartilage (shock absorption, low friction; avascular), synovial membrane (makes synovial fluid, lining, barrier, negative pressure), synovial fluid (nourishes cartilage, lubricates; hyaluronate = viscosity), subchondral bone (modifies compressive forces on cartilage).

cards.prompt: Which joint structure is primarily involved in RA and in OA, and what is the result of each?
cards.answer: RA: synovium. Hyperplastic synovium becomes pannus with angiogenesis and erodes cartilage and bone. OA: all of them (Lec01 poll): a whole-joint disorder of cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, ligaments, menisci and muscle. Failed repair leads to cartilage loss, osteophytes, sclerosis and cysts.

cards.prompt: What are the four steps in approaching a patient with joint pain?
cards.answer: 1) Is it in the joint (articular vs periarticular/non-articular)? 2) How many joints and what distribution? 3) Is there inflammation? 4) Other clues: extra-articular manifestations.

cards.prompt: What are the top three causes of an acute monoarthritis, and what else should you consider?
cards.answer: Infection (septic, bacterial), crystals (gout, CPPD) and blood (hemarthrosis). Also the first joint of a polyarthritis, and an OA flare if non-inflammatory.

cards.prompt: What does symmetry of joint involvement help you decide, and what doesn't it tell you?
cards.answer: Within inflammatory arthritis, symmetry points to seropositive (RA) and asymmetry to seronegative (SpA). It does NOT separate inflammatory from non-inflammatory arthritis.

cards.prompt: Which two physical features are unique to spondyloarthritis, and what are they?
cards.answer: Enthesitis (painful inflammation where tendon/ligament inserts into bone, e.g. Achilles) and dactylitis (whole-digit 'sausage' swelling).

cards.prompt: List the features of inflammatory back pain.
cards.answer: Insidious onset, morning or night stiffness, better with exercise and worse with rest (usually younger than 45, stiffness over 30 min). Responds to NSAIDs.

cards.prompt: Why should serologic tests be ordered only when pre-test probability is at least moderate?
cards.answer: Test utility is highest at intermediate pre-test probability. At low probability most positives are false positives (autoantibodies occur in healthy people), which cause harm and anxiety without changing the diagnosis.

cards.prompt: List causes of a positive ANA other than SLE.
cards.answer: Other SARDs (SSc, Sjögren's, myositis, ~20% of RA), chronic infections (TB, SBE, mono), autoimmune thyroid or liver disease, drugs (procainamide, TNF inhibitors), and healthy people (more with female sex and age).

cards.prompt: Name conditions other than RA that give a positive RF.
cards.answer: Sjögren's, cryoglobulinemia, subacute bacterial endocarditis, hepatitis C, TB, lupus, liver disease (PBC), lung disease (fibrosis, silicosis), malignancy, and healthy people.

cards.prompt: What is the rule of thumb for the upper limit of normal ESR, and what raises ESR besides inflammation?
cards.answer: Men: age/2. Women: (age + 10)/2. Also raised by paraproteins, anemia, age, female sex, pregnancy, diabetes, renal failure, malignancy and tissue damage.

cards.prompt: List the risk factors for septic arthritis.
cards.answer: Recent infection, a portal of entry, a prosthetic joint, a diseased or damaged joint (RA, OA), immunocompromise (drugs, diabetes, liver disease), and age extremes.

cards.prompt: What are the four principles of treating septic arthritis?
cards.answer: 1) Know the organisms (cover S. aureus). 2) Culture synovial fluid and blood first, then empiric IV antibiotics (2–4 wk) and then oral, tailored to sensitivities. 3) Source control: daily aspiration or surgical debridement. 4) Rest, then gentle mobilization with physio.

cards.prompt: Describe Lyme arthritis.
cards.answer: A late feature of Borrelia burgdorferi infection, months after a black-legged tick bite: mono- or oligoarthritis, knee most common. IgG serology should be positive by this stage. Treated with doxycycline.

cards.prompt: What triggers an acute gout attack, and how does acute gout present?
cards.answer: Triggers: medical illness, surgery, drugs, diet/alcohol. Presentation: sudden, intensely painful night-time inflammation, usually of the first MTP; can't bear sheets or weight; recurrent, with normal intervals between attacks.

cards.prompt: When is urate-lowering therapy indicated in gout, and when isn't it?
cards.answer: Indicated: recurrent attacks (≥2/year), tophi or radiographic damage. Consider after a first attack with moderate–severe CKD, very high urate or uric-acid stones. Not after a single uncomplicated attack, and never for asymptomatic hyperuricemia.

cards.prompt: When should you think about a systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease?
cards.answer: Multisystem disease (skin, joint, kidney, muscle, lung) with evidence of inflammation, immune activation, vasculopathy or vasculitis: e.g. inflammatory arthritis + rash + cytopenias + GN + ILD + Raynaud's, with a positive ANA in context.

cards.prompt: Which findings suggest Raynaud's is secondary to a collagen vascular disease?
cards.answer: Digital ischemia (pitting scars, ulcers), abnormal nailfold capillaries, plus other features such as puffy or tight skin, dysphagia, dyspnea or rash. Primary Raynaud's has none of these.

cards.prompt: Distinguish vasculitis from vasculopathy.
cards.answer: Vasculitis: inflammation and necrosis of the vessel wall, leading to hemorrhage or thrombosis (systemic vasculitis). Vasculopathy: endothelial dysfunction with intimal proliferation and luminal narrowing, without inflammation (scleroderma).

cards.prompt: List the history and exam features of giant cell arteritis.
cards.answer: Age >50; new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms (painless vision loss), PMR, constitutional symptoms. Exam: tender, beaded or pulseless temporal artery; arm BP difference >10 mmHg; bruits. Labs: high ESR/CRP and platelets.

cards.prompt: How is fibromyalgia diagnosed?
cards.answer: Clinically: chronic widespread pain for ≥3 months in ≥6 of 9 body sites, with moderate–severe sleep disturbance and/or fatigue. Exam is normal apart from diffuse tenderness. No confirmatory test; investigations only to exclude mimics.

cards.prompt: What initial investigations suit a patient with suspected RA, and why the CBC/Cr/LFTs and CXR?
cards.answer: CBC, creatinine, LFTs, ESR/CRP, RF + anti-CCP, ANA (± ENA/complements), urinalysis + ACR, chest X-ray. CBC/Cr/LFTs show organ involvement and give safe baselines for NSAIDs/DMARDs. CXR finds ILD and is a baseline before methotrexate.

cards.prompt: Why shouldn't the 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria be used as diagnostic criteria?
cards.answer: They're classification criteria built for research (homogeneous study populations) and favour sensitivity. SLE, PsA and parvovirus can score ≥6; true seronegative or early RA can score <6; long-standing inactive RA is classified through the erosive-disease / previous-fulfilment provision, not by scoring. The scoring domains omit erosions, nodules and EAMs.

cards.prompt: What are the key counselling points when starting methotrexate?
cards.answer: Once WEEKLY (not daily); folic acid daily except the MTX day; GI upset and mouth ulcers; liver (limit alcohol), marrow and rare pneumonitis (report cough/dyspnea); infection and no live vaccines; teratogenic, so use specific reliable contraception; avoid TMP-SMX; bloodwork monthly then every 3 months; works in 6–12 weeks.

cards.prompt: What adverse effects and precautions are common to all biologic DMARDs?
cards.answer: Infection risk (including opportunistic, TB and hepatitis B reactivation): screen TB (CXR) and HBV first, vaccinate beforehand, no live vaccines, hold for infection and surgery. Injection or infusion reactions. Anti-TNF: non-melanoma skin cancer.

cards.prompt: Give the boundaries and contents of the axilla.
cards.answer: Apex: clavicle, 1st rib, scapula. Anterior: pectoralis major and minor. Posterior: subscapularis (+ teres major, lats). Medial: thoracic wall + serratus anterior. Lateral: intertubercular sulcus. Base: skin/subcutaneous tissue. Contents: axillary vessels, lymphatics, fat, brachial plexus (axillary sheath).

cards.prompt: Which neurovascular structures are at risk with a surgical-neck humeral fracture, and what deficit results?
cards.answer: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery. Deficit: weak abduction (deltoid) and external rotation (teres minor), with numbness over the lateral shoulder ('regimental badge' area).

cards.prompt: Which anterior forearm muscles are NOT supplied by the median nerve, and which posterior ones don't extend the wrist or digits?
cards.answer: Anterior: flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of FDP (ulnar nerve). Posterior: brachioradialis (flexes the elbow) and supinator (supinates), both radial nerve.

cards.prompt: What are the three pattern questions and the mandatory question in mechanical back pain?
cards.answer: Where is the pain worst (back vs leg)? Is it constant or intermittent (does it ever stop completely)? Does bending forward make it worse? Mandatory: since this pain began, any change in bladder or bowel function (cauda equina)?

cards.prompt: How do physiotherapists and occupational therapists differ in managing MSK disease?
cards.answer: PT: reduce pain and improve mobility, strength and function through exercise, education, self-management, manual therapy and electrotherapy. OT: enable meaningful activity (self-care, work, leisure) with energy conservation, splints, assistive devices and deformity correction. Both are direct-access, but some insurers require a doctor's referral before they cover OT.

cards.answer: 'When you wake up, how long until your joints loosen up to the best they'll be all day?' 30–60 minutes or more suggests inflammatory arthritis; under 30 minutes suggests OA. Also ask about gelling after ≥1 h of immobility. Fibromyalgia can also cause marked stiffness.

cards.prompt: How hard should you press when palpating joints, and what does synovitis feel like compared with an OA node?

cards.prompt: List the six active shoulder movements and how you instruct each.

cards.prompt: How do you palpate PIP and DIP joints for synovitis?
cards.answer: Four-point technique: thumb and index of one hand on the sides of the joint, thumb and index of the other on the top and bottom. Press one pair and feel for fluid moving against the other, then reverse.

cards.prompt: How do you find and palpate the true radiocarpal joint?
cards.answer: Trace the 3rd metacarpal proximally to its base; at the dorsal indentation press with one thumb while feeling for fluid with the other. A normal groove is palpable; synovitis makes it bouncy and fills the groove.
