guides.title: Week 38 · 1 The Synovial Joint & What Arthritis Is
guides.html:
Foundations

The Synovial Joint & What Arthritis Is

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The four tissues that keep a diarthrodial joint healthy, and how inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis damage them in completely different ways.

Anatomy of a diarthrodial (synovial) joint

A healthy joint depends on subchondral bone, articular cartilage, and the synovial membrane/fluid. Disease in any one disrupts the others.

TissueStructureFunction
Articular cartilageAvascular. Chondrocytes + matrix (~80% water + ~20% solids; solids = type II collagen and proteoglycans). Chondrocytes synthesize and maintain the matrix. Smooth hyaline cartilage; zones from the surface: superficial (tangential) → intermediate (transitional) → deep (radial) → tidemark → calcified zone → subchondral bone (SLM06).Resilient, compressible, elastic, self-lubricating: a low-friction, load-bearing surface whose main job is shock absorption.
Synovial membraneIntima: 1–3 layers of synoviocytes (Type A = phagocytic, macrophage-derived; Type B = synthetic, fibroblast-derived). Subintima: vascular fibro-adipose tissue.Low-friction lining; forms synovial fluid; regulates matrix turnover; blood–synovial barrier (semi-permeable, no thick basement membrane, so O2/nutrients pass easily); negative intra-articular pressure aids stability.
Synovial fluidPlasma ultrafiltrate plus locally added hyaluronate (gives viscosity) and lubricin. Normal: clear, viscous, protein 10–25 g/L, <200 WBC ×106/L.Nourishes avascular cartilage, lubricates, forms an adhesive seal.
Subchondral boneBone plate under the cartilage, on a trabecular meshwork.Modifies compressive forces on cartilage. Stiffer bone = more stress on cartilage.
Viscosity = hyaluronate. Shock absorption = cartilage. Synovial fluid is made by the synovium and feeds the cartilage, which has no blood supply of its own: loading presses fluid into the cartilage to reach the chondrocytes (SLM06 narration).

SLM06 quiz: best defence against bacteremia seeding the joint? The synovial membrane, because it holds the phagocytic Type A synoviocytes. The synovium is vascular, so blood-borne bacteria arrive there first; normal synovial fluid has too few WBCs/macrophages to protect the joint (SLM06 narration).

Two categories of joint pathology

Arthritis ("arthro" = joint, "-itis" = inflammation) is a group of >100 conditions causing joint damage, at every age. The first sorting step is always inflammatory vs non-inflammatory.

What inflammation is (PW01)

Part of our normal body defences (innate, then adaptive immunity). PW01: it can be acute (minutes to hours; innate: resident macrophages release cytokines → vascular permeability → fluid, cells and complement enter) or become chronic (adaptive: T and B cells; takes at least a week to gear up, then persists, especially in autoimmunity) (PW01 narration). The five cardinal signs:

LatinSign
RuborRed
DolorPainful
CalorWarm
TumorSwelling
Functio laesaLoss of function

The classification tree (Lec01)

BranchArthritis onlySystemic
Inflammatory: autoimmuneSeropositive (RA), seronegative (SpA)Lupus and other CTDs, vasculitis
Inflammatory: non-autoimmuneCrystal, infectious—
Non-inflammatoryOsteoarthritis; biomechanical (bursa, tendon, other periarticular problems)

Acute inflammatory arthritis

  • Infectious (septic) arthritis: inflammation from bacterial infection
  • Gout: inflammation from monosodium urate crystal deposition

Chronic inflammatory arthritis

  • Rheumatoid arthritis: trigger unknown; becomes chronic through autoimmunity
  • Chronic infection (Lyme, TB, fungal) and many others

Rheumatoid arthritis pathophysiology: a synovial disease

The synovium is the primary target. Early RA shows a hyperplastic synovial membrane (villi) with an influx of neutrophils and T and B cells, so synovial fluid WBC rises (PW01; Lec01). In established RA, synovial proliferation and cell influx continue, the synovium becomes pannus with extensive angiogenesis, and pannus erodes cartilage and bone.

Osteoarthritis: failed repair

OA is "a disease of synovial joints that represents failed repair of joint damage resulting from joint-level or systemic stresses" (synovium, subchondral bone, cartilage, ligaments, menisci) → breakdown of cartilage and bone. There is mild inflammation during attempted repair, but nothing like RA.

"Degenerative" is the old name: it described only the end stage. OA is the final common pathway of many joint stressors; osteophytes are new bone laid down by the failed repair response (PW01 narration).

Lecture poll: which structure does OA primarily involve?
All of them: OA is a whole-joint disorder (bone, cartilage, entheses, synovium), with accelerated breakdown of cartilage, subchondral bone and surrounding tissue plus failed repair. The PW01 knee diagram shows cartilage breakdown, bone remodelling and sclerosis, osteophytes, meniscal damage, synovial hypertrophy, ligament dysfunction, muscle atrophy and altered fat metabolism.

Symptoms and findings side by side

InflammatoryOsteoarthritis
Pain, limited movementPain, limited movement
Warmth, swelling (soft, boggy), ± rednessMinimal or no warmth or swelling
Prolonged morning stiffnessCrepitus, bony deformity
Hands: swollen PIPs with skin folds stretched out, red-purple hue; the valleys between the MCPs fill in (early RA)Hands: hard, shiny bony bumps = osteophytes (Heberden's DIP, Bouchard's PIP) from failed repair; crepitus = audible/palpable noise from damaged structures (PW01/PW03 narration)
X-ray: erosions, periarticular osteopenia, uniform joint-space lossX-ray: non-uniform joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral cysts/sclerosis
Exam discriminator
Erosions (with periarticular osteopenia) are the radiographic change of inflammatory arthritis. Osteophytes and subchondral cysts/sclerosis are OA changes. Joint-space loss occurs in both (uniform in inflammatory arthritis, non-uniform in OA), so on its own it doesn't discriminate (the WFQ Q1 key implies it is OA-only). RA destroys bone and makes no osteophytes; OA remodels and lays down new bone.
Cartilage + synovium + fluid + subchondral bone = a healthy joint. Cardinal signs: rubor, dolor, calor, tumor, functio laesa. RA attacks the synovium (pannus → erosions). OA is a whole-joint disease of failed repair (osteophytes, cysts, meniscus, synovium, muscle). Inflammation = warm, swollen, stiff in the morning; OA = crepitus and deformity.

guides.title: Week 38 · 2 Approach to the Patient with Joint Pain
guides.html:
Algorithm

Approach to the Patient with Joint Pain

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The four-step algorithm (is it the joint, how many, is it inflamed, what other clues), the CBL tutor's refinements, and how to read synovial fluid.

The four steps

StepQuestionHow you answer it
1Is the problem in the joint?Articular: patient localizes to the joint, pain with ALL movements, ± limited range. Periarticular (tendonitis, bursitis, ligament strain): pain in one direction only, the one that stresses the structure. Non-articular: bone (e.g. avascular necrosis), neuropathic, or referred pain (e.g. cholecystitis → right shoulder). Bursae = synovium-lined pouches that stop tendons/ligaments rubbing on bone (PW02 narration).
2How many joints, and where?Mono vs oligo vs poly; symmetry; small vs large; upper vs lower; axial involvement.
3Is there inflammation?Inflammatory symptoms (history) and signs (exam), then synovial fluid if needed.
4Other clues?Extra-articular manifestations (nodules, rash, ulcers, eye, lung). These point to seropositive vs seronegative disease. OA has none, but often has comorbidities: obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes (PW02 narration).

Counting joints

  • Monoarthritis = 1 joint. Think crystal, infection, or blood ("right ~90% of the time").
  • Oligoarthritis = 2–4. Polyarthritis = 5 or more (CBL tutor; the PW02 narration also says "more than four", resolving the slide's "4 or fewer / 4 or more" overlap).
  • Polyarthritis is almost never septic or crystal (CBL tutor; polyarticular gout and CPPD flares do occur in long-standing disease): think viral or autoimmune. Non-inflammatory polyarthritis is essentially just OA. Bacterial arthritis starts as a monoarthritis; if it has spread to several joints the patient is critically unwell (unstable vitals, positive blood cultures, ICU) (ISAL). The commonest infectious polyarthritis is viral (outpatients: viral or gonococcal). Infectious arthritis should resolve within ~2 months; if it lasts longer, think autoimmune, then seropositive vs seronegative (ISAL).

Inflammatory vs non-inflammatory

InflammatoryNon-inflammatory (OA)
Morning stiffnessProlonged. PW02 slide: 45 min+; PW01/PW02 narration: 30–60 min or more. Lecture poll used 45 min (lecturer: “definitely more than 30 minutes, often for hours”); CS guide >30 min; CBL tutor uses >1 hour (30 min can be normal with age or postpartum)Brief; "gelling" after sitting
ActivityBetter with use, worse with rest (the Lec01 poll picked prolonged morning stiffness as the most specific history feature)Worse with use, better with rest
SleepWakes them at 3–6 amTrouble getting to sleep; worse end of day
ExamWarm, soft synovial swelling, ± erythema, effusion, stress painMinimal warmth, bony enlargement, crepitus
SystemicFatigue, fever, weight loss, extra-articular diseaseAbsent
NSAID responseInflammatory pain responds to NSAIDs (CBL tutor: especially useful for inflammatory back pain; many patients can't take them)Less response
Lecture poll: the exam sign most specific for inflammation
Of joint-line tenderness, reduced range of motion, effusion and subluxation, effusion is the most specific. Tenderness and reduced range occur in inflammatory and non-inflammatory disease alike; subluxation means damage.
Three traps from CBL
Symmetry does not separate inflammatory from mechanical. It separates seropositive (symmetric) from seronegative (asymmetric). DIP involvement is an RA-vs-other point (OA and psoriatic arthritis both hit DIPs). Swelling/effusion raises the question but doesn't prove inflammation: OA knees get effusions.

Synovial fluid: an extension of the exam

NormalNon-inflammatoryInflammatorySeptic (typical)
AppearanceClearClearTurbidTurbid, thick
ViscosityHighHighLowLow
WBC ×106/L<200<2,000>2,000>50,000, 80–90% PMN

The 50,000 cut-off is a guideline only: sepsis can occur at lower counts (especially when immunosuppressed) and crystals can push counts higher. A count below 50,000 makes sepsis less likely but does not exclude it: culture decides. The lecturer's rule: "septic arthritis is always inflammatory", so non-inflammatory fluid (<2,000) is not septic; a WBC around 50,000 raises the likelihood of infection but does not prove it.

  • Viscosity falls in inflammation because inflammation breaks down hyaluronic acid.
  • Bedside trick: you can read the numbers on the syringe through clear, non-inflammatory fluid.
  • Inflammatory fluid is turbid because of increased cells and protein (PW02 narration).

Putting it together

MonoarthritisPolyarthritis
Inflammatory: infection (Staph, gonococcal, fungal), crystals (gout, pseudogout), blood (trauma, anticoagulation), first joint of a polyarthritis
Non-inflammatory: OA flare		Inflammatory: infectious (viral, e.g. parvovirus B19; gonococcal), autoimmune (seropositive, seronegative)
Non-inflammatory: OA
"Other" bucket: vasculitis, sarcoid, cryoglobulinemia, paraneoplastic, checkpoint-inhibitor arthritis

Where each disease strikes (PW02 maps)

OsteoarthritisRheumatoid arthritis
Joints (map)DIPs and PIPs, first CMC, hips, knees, first MTP, cervical and lumbar spineMCPs, PIPs, wrists, knees, ankles, MTPs, cervical spine
Highlighted on the slideDIPs and lumbar spineMCPs and MTPs
Pattern (slide)Usually an oligo- or polyarthritis, usually symmetrical; neck and low back can be involvedSymmetrical small- and large-joint polyarthritis; cervical spine only (lumbar spine and DIPs spared)

Why it matters: treatments differ between the forms of arthritis, and early recognition leads to better outcomes. Arthritis is the leading cause of serious chronic disease in Ontario (reported by ~1 million adults) and the number one cause of disability and costs in Canada.

The three PW02 cases

  • 55-year-old, sudden night-time pain in the first MTP, red, swollen → acute inflammatory monoarthritis: gout.
  • 27-year-old woman, 6 months, rings don't fit, 2 h morning stiffness, wrists/fingers/knees → symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis: early RA (cervical, never lumbar spine).
  • 78-year-old, slowly progressive hands and knees since her 50s, stiff for a few steps → chronic non-inflammatory polyarthritis: OA (neck and low back can be involved).
Is it the joint? How many? Inflamed? Other clues? Mono = crystal/infection/blood → aspirate. Poly = viral or autoimmune. Symmetry sorts seropositive from seronegative, not inflammatory from OA. WBC >2,000 inflammatory; >50,000 suggests septic (guideline only).

guides.title: Week 38 · 3 Seropositive vs Seronegative Polyarthritis
guides.html:
Patterns

Seropositive vs Seronegative Polyarthritis

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Two families of inflammatory polyarthritis with different joint patterns, extra-articular manifestations and disease associations, plus PEAR.

The two families

SeropositiveSeronegative (spondyloarthritis, SpA)
DiseasesRheumatoid arthritis (prototype), SLE, inflammatory myositis, scleroderma, MCTD, Sjögren'sPEAR: Psoriatic, Enteropathic (IBD), Ankylosing spondylitis, Reactive; plus undifferentiated SpA
PatternSymmetric, small and large joints, wrists/MCPs, upper and lower limbs. Cervical spine but NOT lumbar or thoracic (PW03 narration)Often asymmetric, oligoarticular, lower-limb; ray involvement; spine and SI joints
Unique featuresNodules, positive RF/anti-CCP or ANAEnthesitis and dactylitis; inflammatory back pain

Older patients with seropositive disease may present with less specific features, and the seropositive pattern can look similar in other SARDs (e.g. lupus with joint involvement).

Historically "seropositive" meant a positive rheumatoid factor. It is now also used for the diseases with other autoantibodies such as ANA. "Seronegative RA" means an RA picture without RF. RF helps confirm RA but isn't required, and a negative RF can't rule RA out (Lec02). Few rules are absolute: PsA can have a positive ANA or RF.

Extra-articular manifestations (EAM)

SiteSeropositiveSeronegative
Skin/mucosaRheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, lupus malar/photosensitive rash, alopecia, dermatomyositis rash, oral ulcers (lupus), Raynaud's, xerostomia (Sjögren's)Psoriasis, erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum (both seen with IBD), mucosal ulcers
EyeEpiscleritis (layer over the sclera); scleritis (the sclera itself; more serious)Iritis/uveitis (red around the iris, anterior chamber inflammation, can scar); conjunctivitis (inflammatory, not infectious)
Internal organsLung, cardiac, renal (may need labs to detect)Bowel inflammation, genitourinary inflammation (urethritis): sterile, UTI symptoms without infection (PW03 narration)

Rheumatoid nodules: hard lumps on extensor surfaces, classically the elbow (always palpate it); vasculitic core with a surrounding granulomatous response, sometimes attached to bone. Vasculitis signs: livedo reticularis (lacy), palpable purpura (small vessel), periungual haemorrhages/infarcts (PW03 narration).

Spondyloarthritis: axial vs peripheral

  • Axial SpA (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis): whole spine from SI joints to neck, plus the "root" joints (shoulders, hips) (PW03 narration). Always ask peripheral-pattern patients about inflammatory back pain. May present only as inflammatory back pain (ISAL): onset <45 y, insidious, >3 months, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise, worse with rest, pain in the second half of the night, alternating buttock pain, very good NSAID response. Lumbar spine and SI inflammation is not a feature of RA or seropositive disease. (More in Week 39.)
  • Peripheral SpA (e.g. psoriatic): asymmetric, lower-extremity, ray pattern = several joints along one digit, not the same joint (MCPs/PIPs) across both hands (PW03 narration).
  • Enthesitis = painful inflammation where tendons/ligaments insert into bone. PW03's map of common SpA enthesitis sites: heels (Achilles/calcaneal insertion), costosternal/costochondral junctions, iliac crests, and the posterior pelvis/lumbosacral spinous processes. Dactylitis = whole-digit "sausage" swelling: small-joint arthritis + osteitis (narration: “inflammation in the covering of the bone”, strictly periostitis) + tendon-sheath inflammation (tenosynovitis), all at once; a good indicator of seronegative disease (PW03 narration).
  • ISAL enthesitis sites: anterior chest wall, pelvic brim, Achilles tendon, plantar fascia. Enthesitis and dactylitis are not seen in seropositive disease.
  • SpA workup (ISAL, only at moderate pre-test probability): ESR/CRP can be normal; if raised, a poor prognostic sign. RF/ANA only with peripheral arthritis (RA or lupus on the differential); not in strictly axial SpA. HLA-B27 has limited sensitivity and specificity (only 1 in 50 carriers develop AS); order it when IBP is present but X-rays are negative, and a positive result may prompt an MRI.
  • SpA imaging (ISAL): SI-joint X-ray shows erosions, sclerosis, partial then complete fusion (grading not needed); lumbar spine shows syndesmophytes. MRI (bone-marrow edema) shows active, reversible inflammation: use it when the history suggests SpA but X-rays are normal, or when activity is unclear on treatment.

The four PEAR diseases

DiseaseKey features
Ankylosing spondylitisSpine, hips, uveitis (PW03 slide; the commonest EAM). IBD also occurs in AS (~19% in the Week 39 SpA lecture)
EnteropathicWith Crohn's/UC and all their EAMs; peripheral arthritis may follow bowel activity; spondylitis runs an independent course (PW03 narration)
PsoriaticBefore or after the psoriasis; several patterns (including monoarthritis and DIP disease); can be very destructive in small joints; nail pitting/onycholysis. About five patterns; nail disease strongly predicts arthritis, especially DIP (PW03 narration)
ReactiveAsymmetric oligoarthritis 1–3 weeks (PW03; the Week 39 lecture and ISAL say 1–4) after certain GI or GU infections, with mucosal ulcers, conjunctivitis, urethritis; enthesitis and dactylitis are common (PW03 narration)
WFQ-style pattern recognition
Asymmetric polyarthritis without spine or SI involvement in a young adult → peripheral SpA (not AS, which needs the axial skeleton; not RA, which is symmetric; not DGI, which is migratory with skin lesions). WFQ Q4 is debatable: its homunculus includes both wrists, both knees and small hand joints, and the answer rests on the one-sided elbow, ankle and forefoot; peripheral SpA is classically an asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis. WFQ Q5 key error: SpA "should not involve the knees" is wrong (peripheral SpA commonly does); the real discriminator there is that her back pain is mechanical.

Why sort them?

Both are inflammatory polyarthritides and some treatment overlaps (peripheral SpA is treated much like RA). But axial SpA skips conventional DMARDs: NSAIDs first, then biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17). Different associations also change what you screen for (eyes, bowel, skin, GU).

Seropositive = RA/CTDs: symmetric small + large joints, cervical not lumbar, nodules, scleritis, Raynaud's. Seronegative = PEAR: asymmetric, lower-limb, axial/SI, enthesitis, dactylitis, uveitis, psoriasis, IBD, post-infectious.

guides.title: Week 38 · 4 Using the Clinical Immunology Lab
guides.html:
Serology

Using the Clinical Immunology Lab

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Pre-test probability, ANA and its subsets, ANCA, RF vs anti-CCP, acute-phase reactants and complements, and what each test can and cannot tell you.

The order of operations

History and physical (most important) → routine labs (show which organs are involved and how urgent it is, and later monitor immunosuppressive drug toxicity) → serology ("icing on the cake"). There is no gold-standard autoantibody test, and autoantibodies occur in healthy people. Autoantibodies often appear years before a SARD, but in one person you can't tell who will stay healthy and who will progress (PW04 narration).

Bayes: order serology only at intermediate pre-test probability

Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP). (Careful: the PW04 narration glosses these as "if positive, has disease" / "if negative, doesn't", which describes PPV/NPV; those depend on pre-test probability, while sensitivity and specificity are fixed properties of the test.) A test's clinical utility is highest when pre-test probability is intermediate. PW04's worked example uses a test with 92% sensitivity and 92% specificity:

Pre-test probabilityPost-test if positivePost-test if negative
10% (low)56%1%
50% (intermediate)92%8%
90% (high)99%43%

At low pre-test a positive result is barely better than a coin toss (56%); at high pre-test a negative result still leaves 43%. Only the intermediate row moves you decisively in both directions. At low prevalence, false positives swamp the result and can distress patient and physician.

ANA

  • Antibodies to nuclear (and some cytoplasmic) antigens. Measured by indirect immunofluorescence on a HEp-2 (human epithelial cell) monolayer with fluorescein-labelled anti-human Ig and serial dilutions (titres 1:40, 1:80, 1:160…; the highest dilution still positive is the titre reported), or by ELISA (many samples at once, so used by many community labs) or bead assays (PW04 narration). Named staining patterns: homogeneous, rim, speckled, nucleolar. Staining patterns are not reliable for diagnosis.
  • Sensitive screen for SLE: 95–100% of SLE is ANA-positive. A negative ANA essentially excludes lupus ("the one real rule").
  • Not specific: other SARDs, chronic infection (TB, SBE, mono), autoimmune thyroid or liver disease, celiac disease, a family history of autoimmune disease, drugs (procainamide, TNF inhibitors), ~20% of RA, and healthy people.
  • "Positive ANA, no symptoms" is one of the commonest rheumatology referrals: screen for symptoms and, if there are none, reassure (CBL tutor).
IF-ANA titre% of normal people positive
≥1:4020–30%
≥1:8010–12%
≥1:1605%
≥1:3203%

Female sex and age raise ANA prevalence. Because up to 30% of healthy people are positive at 1:40, 1:160 is the usual cut-off for a meaningful ANA (~5% of normals) (PW04 narration).

ENA: the specific subsets

Ordering (CBL tutor): in primary care with uncertainty, send the ANA first and the ENA only if it is positive. With high suspicion (e.g. in rheumatology), send them together. Some labs reflex the ENA automatically, so know your local lab. Choosing Wisely Canada (CBL resource): don't order ANA sub-serologies (ENA, anti-dsDNA) without a positive ANA and clinical suspicion; don't use ANA to screen undifferentiated MSK pain; don't repeat RF/anti-CCP to monitor activity; don't order HLA-B27 in a peripheral RA-like picture. The tutor's "send everything" at high suspicion fits: the rules target low pre-test probability. Dr. Yang (ISAL): once the pre-test probability of lupus is moderate, order the panel together (ANA, ENA/dsDNA/Sm, antiphospholipid, C3/C4) rather than one at a time.

AntibodyDisease
Anti-Sm, anti-dsDNASLE (very specific)
Anti-RNPMCTD (also SLE)
Anti-Ro, anti-LaSjögren's (also SLE)
Anti-Scl-70Diffuse scleroderma
Anti-centromereLimited scleroderma (CREST). A patient has Scl-70 or centromere, not both (PW05 narration)
Anti-Jo-1PM/DM, anti-synthetase syndrome (myositis + lung involvement, a particular rash, arthritis)

Myositis-specific antibodies (nice to know) are found in autoimmune myopathy but not in other rheumatic diseases (PW05):

AntibodyAssociation
Mi-2Classic dermatomyositis, acute
SRPSevere, drug-resistant polymyositis with cardiac involvement
p155/140Juvenile DM; cancer in adult DM
MDA5DM with skin disease, minimal muscle involvement, acute progressive ILD
HMGCRNecrotizing myopathy

ANCA

c-ANCA → anti-PR3 (proteinase 3); p-ANCA → anti-MPO (myeloperoxidase). Immunofluorescence lacks specificity, so ELISA must confirm. The antigens sit in neutrophil granules; the clinically important result is the anti-PR3 or anti-MPO ELISA. Association: the small-vessel ("ANCA") vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA; see the vasculitis guide) (PW05 narration).

RF vs anti-CCP

Rheumatoid factorAnti-CCP (ACPA)
WhatIgM (sometimes IgG) against the Fc of IgGIgG against citrullinated peptides
Sensitivity~60–80% (standard figure); ~20% (PW05) to 20–30% (CBL prep) of RA stays seronegative~68% (similar)
SpecificityPoor (~80–85%, standard figure; PW05 says only “neither specific nor sensitive”)~95%
PredictsExtra-articular manifestations (nodules, ulcers, vasculitis, lung); high titre → aggressive, erosive diseaseErosions (CBL tutor: both RF and anti-CCP predict disease course and EAMs)
Other positivesSjögren's, cryoglobulinemia, SBE, hepatitis C, TB, lupus, myositis, scleroderma, malignancy, liver/lung disease, healthy peopleRare

Positive RF but it doesn't look like RA? Think cryoglobulinemia (immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold, in digital and renal small vessels), SBE and hepatitis C (PW05 narration).

CBL extras: RF makes up the cryoglobulin in 2 of the 3 cryoglobulin types; RF can flip between positive and negative; following an RF titre is useful only in cryoglobulinemia.

Monitoring and when to order
RF and anti-CCP are not useful for monitoring disease activity. Order them once, in someone with swollen joints. Lecture framing: at moderate pre-test probability. The CBL tutor also orders them when suspicion is high, because they add prognostic information (a more aggressive course, erosions, EAMs).

Acute-phase reactants

  • ESR = how far RBCs settle in 1 hour in a 200 mm tube (mm/h). Normally their negative charges make them repel each other and fall slowly; positively charged acute-phase proteins neutralize that charge → RBCs aggregate and fall faster. Also raised by paraproteins, anemia (fewer cells, less repulsion), age, female sex, pregnancy, diabetes, renal failure, malignancy, tissue damage. ULN: men = age/2; women = (age + 10)/2.
  • CRP: made by the liver; responds faster, less affected by irrelevant factors; may be the more sensitive test in some cases. It is driven mainly by the innate immune system, so other immune pathways can cause inflammation without raising it (CBL tutor).
  • Other acute-phase reactants: ferritin, haptoglobin, fibrinogen.
  • Neither reliably separates inflammatory from non-inflammatory joint disease on its own, and a normal CRP does not exclude inflammatory arthritis. A good physical exam should decide whether to order them.

Complement (C3, C4)

Low in immune-complex disease (the complexes activate the cascade and consume C3/C4; levels rise again as disease settles, in many but not all lupus patients, PW05 narration). A biomarker of lupus activity (with anti-dsDNA, the only lupus labs that move with activity; ANA and RF don't change over time). In a sick patient with known lupus, a rising dsDNA and falling complement favour a flare over infection (Lec02), though sepsis can also lower complement.

The two worked quizzes

  • 25-year-old, arthritis + rash + fevers: start with CBC, creatinine, urinalysis (cytopenias, 1+ blood/protein) → ANA 1:640 → ENA (anti-dsDNA+, Ro+) → low C3/C4 = active lupus; also send antiphospholipid antibodies if never measured. (The slide prints C4 as 0.8 g/L against a 0.12–0.55 range, a typo: the narrator says both C3 and C4 were low.)
  • 46-year-old with thumb CMC, PIP, DIP and knee pain with use, 10 min stiffness, RF 178: low pre-test probability, so she has OA, not RA. ESR 25 is normal for her: (46 + 10)/2 = 28.
Routine labs first. ANA = sensitive screen for SLE (negative excludes). ENA for specificity: Sm/dsDNA = SLE, Scl-70 = diffuse, centromere = limited, Jo-1 = anti-synthetase. Anti-CCP is the specific RA test (erosions); RF predicts EAMs. Neither monitors activity. Low C3/C4 + rising dsDNA = active lupus.

guides.title: Week 38 · 5 Septic Arthritis
guides.html:
Don't Miss

Septic Arthritis

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The one don't-miss cause of monoarthritis: how bacteria reach the joint, who is at risk, gonococcal and Lyme variants, diagnosis, and treatment principles.

Why it matters

Acute bacterial infection of a joint is potentially life-threatening, with adult mortality of 10–50%. Delayed treatment destroys cartilage and bone (a lifetime of disability). In any acute monoarthritis, always consider infection.

Pathogenesis and organisms

  • Most common route: hematogenous seeding from another infection (pneumonia, pyelonephritis, skin infection, infective endocarditis).
  • Gram-positive cocci 75–80%; gram-negative bacilli 15–20%.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism, which is why empiric therapy must cover it.
  • Consider streptococci (especially group B) and gram-negatives in elderly and immunocompromised adults; a different profile in children; N. gonorrhoeae if sexually active or at risk of sexual abuse (including youth and older adults).

Risk factors

Risk factorExample
Recent infectionPneumonia, UTI, cellulitis, endocarditis
Portal of entrySkin breaks, injection, IV drug use (Lec01's examples: an accident, a knife wound, stepping on something sharp weeks earlier)
Prosthetic jointHip or knee replacement
Diseased/damaged jointRA, OA, prior crystal disease
ImmunocompromiseImmunosuppressive drugs (biologics), diabetes, chronic liver disease
Age extremesElderly and the very young

Presentation

  • Knee and hip most common, but any joint can be infected.
  • Can be insidious in the elderly and immunosuppressed (and biologics blunt fever and inflammation).
  • Can masquerade as a "flare": one joint out of proportion in someone with known RA is a red flag for infection.

Gonococcal arthritis

  • Typically young, healthy adults; incidence is rising.
  • Two forms: (1) typical septic monoarthritis; (2) disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) with migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis and a few hemorrhagic pustules on the limbs (not the trunk).
  • Culture the sites where gonococcus enters: oropharynx, urethra, cervix/vagina, rectum.

Chronic infective monoarthritis

Syphilis (rising again), Lyme disease, osteo-articular TB, fungi (e.g. sporotrichosis). With more patients immunosuppressed (transplants, immune checkpoint therapy), unusual chronic infections such as TB and fungi are seen more often. There are also immune-mediated post-infectious arthritides (reactive).

Lyme arthritis
The commonest feature of late infection with Borrelia burgdorferi (black-legged tick), usually months after the bite. Three stages (lecture): (1) erythema migrans with flu-like aches; (2) neurologic and cardiac involvement, disseminated rash, migratory aches; (3) late chronic mono- or oligoarthritis, knee most common. By the arthritis stage patients should be IgG-seropositive (early serology can be negative). The lecture case was treated with doxycycline for a month. Ask about hiking, woods and tick exposure.

Diagnosis

  • Synovial aspiration: Gram stain, culture and sensitivity (plus cell count and crystals). Aspiration is an extension of the physical exam.
  • Blood cultures are frequently positive: always draw them.
  • GC cultures from mucosal sites when relevant.
  • X-ray: late cartilage and bone destruction if treatment is delayed.

Treatment principles

#Principle
1Know the organisms: cover S. aureus; broaden for strep/gram-negatives in the elderly/immunocompromised; think GC in the sexually active.
2Culture first (synovial fluid + blood), then empiric IV antibiotics (per local ID guidelines), then tailor to sensitivities. IV for ~2–4 weeks, then oral. Why first: after about 24 h of antibiotics cultures can turn falsely negative while the infection is still uncontrolled.
3Source control / decompression: the standard of care is arthroscopic debridement by orthopedics; daily aspiration is the fallback where orthopedics isn't available, until transfer. The infection is enclosed, so it must be drained even though antibiotics penetrate the joint well (gout, by contrast, doesn't need repeat aspiration).
4Rest the joint acutely, then gentle mobilization with physiotherapy.
Classic wrong answer
An 88-year-old with a swollen wrist given a week of oral cephalexin at a walk-in clinic was undertreated. If you are going to treat septic arthritis, treat properly: cultures, IV antibiotics, source control. Without a clear alternative explanation, you may need to treat empirically until cultures are negative. (His real diagnosis was pseudogout; see the crystal guide.)
Hot single joint = septic until proven otherwise. Hematogenous, S. aureus most common, knee/hip. Risk: prosthesis, damaged joint, immunosuppression (biologics), age. Aspirate (Gram, culture, count, crystals) + blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics, then empiric IV → tailor, and drain the joint. DGI = migratory arthritis + tenosynovitis + pustules in a young adult.

guides.title: Week 38 · 6 Crystal Arthritis & the Monoarthritis Workup
guides.html:
Gout · CPPD

Crystal Arthritis & the Monoarthritis Workup

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Gout, pseudogout and hydroxyapatite compared; the other causes of monoarthritis; and the 3 C's you will be asked about in clerkship and PGY1.

Gout

A primary disorder of urate metabolism. Adenine → hypoxanthine → xanthine; guanine → xanthine; xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine → xanthine and xanthine → uric acid (Lec01); exists mainly as monosodium urate. High serum urate deposits crystals around joints; crystals shed into the joint are phagocytosed by neutrophils (drawn in by complement activation; crystal-induced neutrophil lysis releases lysosomal enzymes, LTB4, prostaglandins and free radicals) and monocytes (IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8) → intense inflammation.

Urate balance and risk factors (Lec01 slide 68)

InputOutput
~30% diet (purines); ~70% the body's own nucleotide turnover (raised in obesity)~70% kidney; ~30% gut

Risk factors for poor renal excretion: genetics, metabolic syndrome (HTN, insulin resistance, hyperlipidemia), renal impairment, and drugs that reduce renal urate handling such as diuretics. Crystals deposit more readily in joints with OA and with ageing.

Acute gout

  • First MTP most commonly (podagra); other lower-extremity joints; any joint in long-standing disease.
  • Intensely painful, onset in the middle of the night, can't bear sheets or weight.
  • Recurrent, normal between attacks. Triggers: medical illness, surgery, drugs, diet/alcohol.
  • Untreated, an attack resolves on its own (about 10 days); it is painful but not life-threatening.
  • Who: in older patients, especially women, gout can involve the hand and wrist. Gout is uncommon in young women (unless CKD or a genetic cause), so first-MTP "gout" in a young woman is more likely hydroxyapatite.

Chronic gout

Escalating attacks over years → persistent destructive arthritis and tophi (tissue deposits of monosodium urate). Look for tophi on the toes, fingers (older patients) and the olecranon bursa/elbow. Tophi mean too much urate in the body: they need urate-lowering therapy, and they gradually shrink and disappear with it (surgery only if bulky or interfering with footwear). X-ray: punched-out erosions with an "overhanging edge".

Diagnosis

Clinical picture + hyperuricemia is only presumptive. Synovial analysis confirms: needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals, intracellular in PMNs during an attack. Always culture too: crystals and infection can coexist. (Compensator mechanics are nice-to-know.) The lecturer said a quick response to colchicine suggests gout (Lec01). That is overstated: colchicine is also used in CPPD (less helpful acutely, can be tried in chronic CPPD), so a response doesn't prove gout; only crystals confirm it.

The three crystal arthropathies

GoutCPPD (pseudogout)Hydroxyapatite
WhoMiddle-aged men, risk factorsOlder (>60)Younger, not at risk for gout/CPPD
JointsFirst toe, lower-extremityWrist, knee (not first toe)Shoulder (supraspinatus tendon), hip, first MTP in a young woman
CourseRecurrentOften a one-offRandom
CrystalsNeedle, negatively birefringentRod/rhomboid, weakly positively birefringentNot seen on routine microscopy
X-rayErosions (chronic)Chondrocalcinosis (suggestive, not diagnostic)Periarticular calcification
Acute RxNSAID, colchicine, glucocorticoidNSAID, glucocorticoid (colchicine less helpful)NSAID (± glucocorticoid)
PreventionLifestyle + urate-lowering therapyNothing available (colchicine can be tried for chronic CPPD)Nothing available
Periarthritis vs arthritis
Acute calcific periarthritis of the shoulder (hydroxyapatite in the supraspinatus tendon): the patient can't abduct, and active movement is too painful, but the examiner can move the joint passively, and glenohumeral rotation with the elbow at the waist is painless. In a true monoarthritis, passive movement is also impossible.

Managing gout: three goals

  1. Treat the acute flare: ice, rest, splint + colchicine (only early: within 12–36 h per SLM01; Lec01 says “early in the attack”; ISAL: works best within ~48 h, less likely to work by ~day 5) or an NSAID (if no HTN, CKD, CHF, ulcer risk; stop after ~7–10 days) or a glucocorticoid (oral, or intra-articular only once you're confident the joint isn't infected). Colchicine isn't continued after an attack resolves (unless as ULT flare cover). If NSAIDs are contraindicated and it's too late for colchicine: inject a single joint (only local side effects); with two joints you can inject both; with a polyarticular flare use oral glucocorticoids (ISAL).
  2. Prevent attacks and 3. prevent chronic disease: lifestyle (limit alcohol, especially beer, purines/red and organ meat, high-fructose corn syrup, weight loss) and urate-lowering therapy (ULT).
Start ULT whenDon't start ULT when
Recurrent attacks (≥2/year on the lecture slide and in SLM01; the WFQ key and the lecturer's spoken wording say >2/year), chronic gout/tophi, or radiographic damage. Consider after a first attack if moderate–severe CKD, very high urate, or uric-acid stones.After a first attack otherwise: monitor for further attacks and give a prescription for colchicine to use at the next attack if renal function is normal (WFQ Q12). Never treat asymptomatic hyperuricemia.

Allopurinol titrated to serum urate <360 µmol/L (lower with tophi), continued indefinitely, with flare prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine/NSAID/prednisone) at the start. Gout is managed in primary care; referral isn't routinely needed.

Other causes of monoarthritis

  • Hemarthrosis: traumatic, or non-traumatic with coagulopathy/anticoagulants or other joint pathology. Now mostly managed conservatively: leave it and mobilize the joint to avoid adhesions (aspirating and injecting steroid is no longer standard).
  • First presentation of a polyarthritis: usually subacute; evolves with follow-up.
  • OA "flare": minimal inflammation, less disabling than crystals.

The approach: 3 C's

History and exam (risk factors for infection, crystals, bleeding) → aspirate → Culture, Cell count, Crystals. If you only get a little fluid, culture is the priority. Then treat the inflammation (drugs chosen for the individual's comorbidities) and treat infection properly if suspected, following up cultures either way.

The Mr. C resolution
88-year-old, 10-day swollen wrist: WBC 34,000 (89% PMN), positively birefringent crystals, culture negative, chondrocalcinosis on X-ray → acute pseudogout, treated with an intra-articular glucocorticoid. The steroid was given only because the team was confident it wasn't infection. With infection risk factors: admit, give empiric IV antibiotics, wait for negative cultures, then treat as CPPD.
Mono = infection, crystal, blood (+ first joint of a polyarthritis, OA flare). 3 C's, culture first. Gout: first MTP, night, recurrent, needle-shaped negative crystals; colchicine early, NSAID or steroid; ULT only for recurrent attacks/tophi/damage (not after one attack, never for asymptomatic urate). CPPD: older, wrist/knee, rhomboid positive crystals, chondrocalcinosis.

guides.title: Week 38 · 7 Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases
guides.html:
SLE · Myositis · SSc

Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The principles of autoimmunity, then the three collagen vascular diseases you must recognize: SLE, inflammatory myositis and systemic sclerosis.

Five principles of autoimmune disease (SLM05)

  1. Results from failure or breakdown of tolerance in B cells, T cells, or both (SLM05). Lec02 adds that tolerance fails centrally and peripherally and that the adaptive immune system plays the greatest role. (Autoinflammatory diseases are different: genetic and driven by the innate immune system. Strictly, "connective tissue disease" means inborn collagen disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers–Danlos, so Lec02 prefers "SARD".)
  2. Driven by genetic susceptibility + environmental triggers. Many rheumatic autoimmune diseases have an HLA association; triggers can cause epigenetic changes. Some autoimmunity is normal; disease comes when regulation fails (SLM05 narration).
  3. Immune effector mechanisms (the same ones that fight infection) cause the tissue injury.
  4. Can be organ-specific (type 1 DM, Graves') or systemic (SLE, RA).
  5. Tend to be chronic and progressive: autoantigens are rarely eliminated, and damage exposes new self-antigens.

Four mechanisms of injury

MechanismClassic example
Autoantibodies against self (recruit cells, fix complement)Immune thrombocytopenia (antibody-coated platelets cleared by splenic macrophages via the Fc portion), autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Immune complexes depositing in organsGlomerulonephritis, cutaneous vasculitis (low C3/C4). Soluble antigens complex with antibody and lodge in small vessels, so any organ can be hit: kidney, joints, skin, lung (SLM05 narration)
Autoreactive T cells (CD4 Th1/Th17 cytokines recruit inflammatory cells; CD8 CTLs kill self tissue directly. Th2/T follicular helper cells drive B cells → plasma cells; antibodies opsonize and fix complement)Myositis (CD8+ or CD4+ driven)
CombinationsSLE

When to think of a collagen vascular disease

A cluster: inflammatory arthritis, certain rashes, myositis, glomerulonephritis, cytopenias, ILD, Raynaud's, plus a positive ANA in that context. SARDs are multisystem, inflamed, often autoantibody-positive, and may be undifferentiated at first. A patient can present with one obvious feature (e.g. ILD) and evolve into a full SARD over time: shared early features (cytopenias, rash, vasculopathy, arthritis, Raynaud's, lung disease) sort into RA, lupus, myositis or scleroderma as the antibody profile appears. A respirologist seeing ILD should think of a SARD and test muscle strength. Routine labs show organ involvement and urgency; serology complements.

Systemic lupus erythematosus: "RASH OR PAIN"

LetterFeature
RRash (not always red: it can look different in darker skin, flat or papular): acute cutaneous (malar/butterfly over cheeks, nose and upper lip, sparing the nasolabial folds; red cheeks alone aren't a malar rash), subacute cutaneous (red, raised, scaly, non-scarring, sun-exposed; can look like psoriasis), discoid (chronic red–purple thickened plaques that scar: typically the bowl of the ear, also face and scalp → scarring hair loss); alopecia
AArthritis: non-erosive, peripheral
SSerositis: pleural, pericardial, peritoneal
HHematologic: any cytopenia (hemolysis, low WBC, low platelets). Lupus is one of the few rheumatic diseases that lowers counts; most inflammatory diseases raise platelets or WBC
OOral/nasopharyngeal ulcers
RRenal: glomerulonephritis (HTN, edema, hematuria/proteinuria, AKI/CKD)
PPhotosensitivity: a real rash in sun-exposed areas (face, upper shoulders, neck), not just burning easily
AANA
IImmunologic: anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, antiphospholipid, low C3/C4
NNeurologic: seizure, psychosis

Most worrisome: hematologic, renal, neurologic. Most specific labs: anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, low C3/C4. Only anti-dsDNA and complement change with activity. Antiphospholipid antibodies (against negatively charged phospholipids and their bound proteins; venous and arterial thrombosis, early pregnancy loss; in ~30% of lupus, PW05 narration) are nice to know. Renal disease can be asymptomatic: everyone you suspect has lupus needs a creatinine and urinalysis, and in a known lupus patient with a suspected flare they are the key test (no exam finding detects GN).

Inflammatory myositis

  • Painless, proximal weakness over weeks to months (can't climb stairs, rise from a chair, lift arms), ± dysphagia, cardiac involvement.
  • Extra-muscular: ILD (can be serious), joints, and skin: dermatomyositis rashes are photosensitive; the classic ones cause swelling and redness around the eyes (heliotrope) and over the knuckles (Gottron's).
  • Diagnosis: raised CK + weakness (lecture example: normal ~150, myositis ~3,000), myositis-specific antibodies (± ANA), MRI, EMG, muscle biopsy (interstitial mononuclear infiltrate, myocyte necrosis).
  • Necrotic muscle can regenerate: patients are encouraged to keep using their muscles with gentle physiotherapy. Myositis can also be a feature of SLE and other SARDs.

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)

Not primarily inflammatory by presentation: the hallmarks are vasculopathy and fibrosis (endothelial damage + fibroblast activation).

  • Vasculopathy: Raynaud's (white → blue → red); digital ischemia/pitting and abnormal nailfold capillaries mean secondary Raynaud's; telangiectasia (little red blobs/squares on the face, palms/digits, sometimes the mouth; unlike spider angiomas, which have a central arteriole with radiating vessels); pulmonary arterial hypertension; renal crisis (severe HTN, AKI, TMA).
  • Primary Raynaud's occurs in normal people without vasculopathy (the lecturer estimated ~10% of the class): onset as a teen or young adult with cold exposure and none of the secondary signs. Many people over-report it, so show the patient a picture when you ask.
  • Fibrosis: puffy then tight skin, sclerodactyly (fingers pulled into flexion, painful ulcers over the flexion points), facial tightening (can't close the lips, wrinkles disappear), calcinosis (from ischemia; painful, can ulcerate), ILD, GI reflux and bowel dysmotility (constipation).
SubsetSkinDominant featureAntibody
Limited (CREST)Hands, faceVasculopathy: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, TelangiectasiaAnti-centromere
DiffuseWidespreadFibrosis (skin, lung)Anti-Scl-70

Vasculitis vs vasculopathy

Vasculitis = inflammation and necrosis of vessels (systemic vasculitis). Vasculopathy = endothelial dysfunction with intimal proliferation and narrowing, no inflammation (scleroderma).

Other CTDs (nice to know)

Sjögren's: sicca (anti-Ro/La). Undifferentiated CTD: early, ANA+ without a specific antibody. Overlap (e.g. RA + lupus, "rhupus"): the CBL tutor's approach is to treat the manifestations, after first learning typical RA and typical lupus. MCTD: SLE + SSc + myositis + RA features, anti-RNP.

Management principles

Assess extent of organ involvement (this sets intensity). Glucocorticoids are usually initial therapy, replaced by a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant long-term. The exception is scleroderma: it is fibrotic and vasculopathic rather than inflammatory, so steroids aren't its treatment (Lec02). Moderate/high-dose glucocorticoids are generally avoided in SSc because they raise the risk of scleroderma renal crisis (standard). Manage comorbidities: osteoporosis, HTN, CV risk, depression. Many patients are young women; treat the whole person.

Autoimmunity = failed tolerance, genes + environment, chronic. ITP = antibody-mediated; GN and skin vasculitis = immune complex. SLE: RASH OR PAIN, dsDNA/Sm/low C3-C4. Myositis: painless proximal weakness, high CK. SSc: vasculopathy + fibrosis; limited = centromere/CREST, diffuse = Scl-70. Raynaud's + new dyspnea = think SARD with lung involvement.

guides.title: Week 38 · 8 Non-Articular Pain, PMR, GCA & Fibromyalgia
guides.html:
Non-Articular

Non-Articular Pain, PMR, GCA & Fibromyalgia

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

When MSK pain isn't arthritis: local periarticular problems, the generalized differential, polymyalgia rheumatica, giant cell arteritis and other vasculitis, and fibromyalgia.

Local non-articular pain

Periarticular: bursitis (e.g. prepatellar bursitis: well-circumscribed swelling superficial to the patella, knee joint uninvolved), tendonitis, ligament strain, fracture, avascular necrosis.

Generalized non-articular pain: the differential

CategoryExamples
RheumatologicPMR; inflammatory myositis (more often weakness than pain)
Metabolic / endocrineHypercalcemia; hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism
MalignancyMultiple myeloma, bone metastases
InfectionViral: COVID-19, influenza, hepatitis, HIV
NeurologicMyopathy
DrugsStatins, aromatase inhibitors, bisphosphonates
Central sensitizationFibromyalgia

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)

  • Inflammatory condition in adults ≥50.
  • Pain and morning stiffness (≥30 min) in ≥2 of: shoulder girdle, neck, hip girdle. Trouble raising arms overhead, getting out of a chair.
  • No other inflammatory joint disease; ± constitutional symptoms; no true weakness (pain limits testing).
  • Labs: high ESR and CRP, anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis; RF and anti-CCP negative.
  • Treatment: low–medium dose oral glucocorticoid; referral to rheumatology.
PMR vs myositis
A 48-year-old who can't climb stairs but has no pain or stiffness has myositis (painless weakness), not PMR (pain + stiffness, and she is under 50).

Vasculitis

Inflammation and necrosis of a vessel → perforation/hemorrhage or thrombosis/ischemia/infarction. Mechanisms: cell-mediated, immune-complex, ANCA-associated.

Collagen vascular diseases (and RA)Systemic vasculitis
SerologySeropositive: characteristic antibody profilesNot seropositive; an antibody is seen in only one group (ANCA)
OrgansCharacteristic organ patternsVessel size determines organ involvement
VasculitisCan have small-vessel vasculitis, but it isn't the primary problemThe primary problem
  • Suspect it in a constitutionally ill patient (fever, weight loss, malaise) with multisystem disease. Most common organs: kidney, lung, nerve, skin; often progressive/additive.
  • Vessel size predicts the picture (SLM02 "Vasculitis is a multisystem disease"):
SizeDiseases (Chapel Hill)Clinical features
LargeGCA, TakayasuAorta and main branches: aneurysm, dissection, stenosis (chest pain, limb claudication); CNS: stroke, TIA
MediumPAN, KawasakiSkin: nodules, livedo, digital ulcers, digital gangrene; nerve: mononeuritis multiplex (e.g. wrist drop); gut: mesenteric vasculitis (post-prandial abdominal pain); kidney: renovascular hypertension
SmallANCA: GPA, MPA, EGPA. Immune complex: anti-GBM, cryoglobulinemic, IgA vasculitis, hypocomplementemic urticarial (anti-C1q)Skin: palpable purpura, urticaria, splinter hemorrhages; eye: scleritis; ENT: sinusitis, epistaxis, otitis; lung: alveolar hemorrhage; kidney: glomerulonephritis
  • Palpable purpura → screen other organs, especially the kidney (urinalysis).
  • Treatment: glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (SLM02); SLM01 lists rituximab as the biologic for vasculitis (standard in ANCA vasculitis).
  • ANCA red flags (Lec02, nice to know but "don't miss"): hemoptysis + hematuria + rising creatinine = pulmonary-renal syndrome, a medical emergency. Infographic extras: “ELGN” (ENT, Lung, GN, Neuropathy); PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) → GPA, MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) → MPA; ENT disease suggests GPA; ANCA alone doesn't make the diagnosis (nice to know).

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis): need to know

Large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches; the most common vasculitis in adults >50. ~20% of PMR has GCA; ~40% of GCA has PMR.

HistoryExamLabs / test
New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms (diplopia, painless vision loss, the most serious complication), PMR, constitutional symptoms; rarely aortitis or arm claudicationTender, prominent, beaded or pulseless temporal artery; visual abnormality; arm BP difference >10 mmHg; carotid/subclavian bruitsHigh ESR (>50) and CRP (>10 per the algorithm), anemia, high platelets. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard (a day procedure, done by plastic surgery)
Don't wait: GCA algorithm (CRAJ 2022)
Age ≥50 required. Symptom boxes: new or worsening headache (± scalp tenderness; the key symptom), painless vision loss, PMR (hip and shoulder girdle pain and stiffness), jaw claudication (pain after a few minutes of chewing, not TMJ), fever/weight loss/fatigue. Labs: CBC (high platelets), CRP >10, ESR >50. Headache + abnormal labs, or ≥2 symptom boxes + abnormal labs → oral prednisone 1 mg/kg. Visual loss → 1 g IV pulse methylprednisolone. Call rheumatology (urgent), and ophthalmology if visual symptoms. Start steroids before the biopsy to prevent irreversible blindness. Biologics are used for select patients with GCA (SLM02).

Fibromyalgia

  • Chronic widespread pain ≥3 months with moderate–severe sleep disturbance and/or fatigue.
  • 2019 AAPT: pain in ≥6 of 9 sites (head, both arms, chest, abdomen, upper back, lower back, both legs). Insidious, aching, subjective swelling/stiffness, burning, tingling.
  • Also mood disorder, cognitive impairment, diffuse tenderness, weight gain (not loss). Can follow physical or psychological trauma. Can coexist with rheumatic, neurological or psychiatric illness and other chronic overlapping pain conditions (e.g. endometriosis).
  • Acute-onset pain should raise concern for an alternative explanation.
  • Causes: genetics, environmental triggers and central sensitization (hyper-responsive dorsal horn, reduced descending modulation, excess excitatory transmitters/NMDA activation).
  • History should cover polysymptomatic distress and the impact on function.
  • Exam: diffuse tenderness, otherwise normal (no synovitis). No confirmatory test; limit investigations to real mimics. History, exam and basic bloodwork (CBC, calcium, SPEP, TSH, ESR/CRP, CK) exclude the widespread-pain differential, and all should be normal in fibromyalgia (ISAL). Repeated testing fosters passivity and dependence.
  • Management is multimodal with an emphasis on non-pharmacologic therapy: education, exercise, CBT, sleep (more effective than drugs); then duloxetine or pregabalin. Not NSAIDs or opioids (ineffective; opioids may worsen it).
PMR: ≥50, shoulder/hip girdle stiffness, high ESR/CRP, no weakness, low-dose steroid. GCA: ≥50 + headache/jaw claudication/vision → prednisone 1 mg/kg now (IV pulse if vision lost), biopsy is gold standard. Vasculitis: sick + multisystem; purpura → check urine. Fibromyalgia: ≥3 months, ≥6/9 sites, sleep/fatigue, normal exam; exercise/CBT first, no opioids/NSAIDs.

guides.title: Week 38 · 9 Rheumatoid Arthritis (CBL 38)
guides.html:
CBL · Alex

Rheumatoid Arthritis (CBL 38)

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Alex's case end to end: why it's RA, the workup, RF/anti-CCP interpretation, the 2010 classification criteria, extra-articular disease, X-ray findings, and the septic knee a year later.

The case

Alex, 33, 3 months of hand, wrist, knee and foot pain: ~1 h morning stiffness, better with movement, rings tight, night waking, sicca. Exam: synovitis of wrists, MCP2–5, PIP2–5, knees, MTP2–5, and a red right eye painful on movement with normal acuity.

What to ask (the tutor's additions to the HPI)

  • Onset and pattern; "Has this ever happened before?"
  • "What do you think is going on?" (patients with lupus are often accurate about their own flares)
  • Triggers: viral contacts (a child in daycare: parvovirus); reactive-arthritis exposures: sexual history, travel, GI illness, chlamydia symptoms
  • Is the naproxen working, and is it tolerated?
  • Pregnancy plans (they shape the DMARD choice)
  • Ask about specific review-of-systems items by name rather than "anything else?"

Why RA

  • Symmetric, small-joint-predominant polyarthritis of hands and wrists with demonstrable synovitis.
  • No inflammatory back pain or SI pain (against SpA); few lupus features.
  • Age/sex fit (peak 30–50, F:M ~2–3:1).
  • Duration >3 months argues against parvovirus B19 (the commonest viral RA-mimic, classically in a parent of a daycare child; the tutor says it lasts <3 months, typically 6–8 weeks). Alex's onset was "about three months ago", right at the boundary, so the exclusion is soft.
  • Extra-articular: sicca and probable scleritis. Remember Sjögren's in the seropositive differential.

Workup

CBC, creatinine, liver enzymes (organ involvement + safe baselines for NSAIDs/DMARDs), ESR/CRP, RF + anti-CCP, ANA (→ ENA, dsDNA, complements), urinalysis + urine ACR, chest X-ray (RA-ILD; baseline before methotrexate). Before a biologic: TB screen (IGRA + CXR), hepatitis B, vaccines.

Alex: normocytic anemia, normal ESR/CRP, RF 200, anti-CCP 80 (ULN 20), ANA negative (lupus excluded). Normal inflammatory markers do not rule out RA.

RF and anti-CCP: disease course, not disease activity

  • RF = IgM against IgG Fc (a multivalent pentamer that binds several IgGs). Anti-CCP = IgG against citrullinated proteins (arginine → citrulline by PAD; linked to smoking and HLA-DRB1 shared epitope; can precede arthritis by years).
  • Titres do not track activity (don't repeat them), but high titres predict a more aggressive course, erosions and extra-articular disease. Seropositive patients need tighter control and are more likely to stay on DMARDs.
  • Don't order them in someone without swollen joints.
  • RA is a clinical diagnosis. Serology supports it and adds prognosis but isn't required: if you're ~90% sure of RA and both are negative, the diagnosis stands and it predicts a less aggressive course (tutor). A positive RF alone is not RA.

2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria

Apply only to ≥1 joint with definite synovitis not better explained by another disease. ≥6/10 = definite RA.

DomainPoints
Joints: 1 large / 2–10 large / 1–3 small / 4–10 small / >10 (≥1 small)0 / 1 / 2 / 3 / 5
Serology: both negative / low-positive / high-positive (>3× ULN)0 / 2 / 3
Acute-phase reactants: both normal / either abnormal0 / 1
Duration: <6 weeks / ≥6 weeks0 / 1

Alex = 5 + 3 + 0 + 1 = 9. More than 10 swollen joints (≥1 small) for ≥6 weeks alone reaches 6. Formal small joints: MCPs, PIPs, thumb IP, MTP2–5, wrists (DIPs, first CMC and first MTP excluded). Large joints: shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, ankles. The spine isn't in the criteria: it is axial, which points to seronegative disease. Classification criteria are for research (homogeneous populations), not diagnosis: SLE, PsA and parvovirus can score ≥6; seronegative or early RA can score <6; long-standing inactive RA is classified through the criteria's erosive-disease / previous-fulfilment provision rather than by scoring.

Extra-articular manifestations

SystemManifestation
SkinRheumatoid nodules (granulomatous; histologically characteristic), rheumatoid vasculitis (presents in many ways)
EyeSicca, episcleritis (superficial, painless on movement), scleritis (painful, urgent ophthalmology), retinitis
LungPleuritis/effusion, nodules, ILD, obstructive lung disease
HeartPericarditis; myocarditis (rare: most myocarditis is viral); accelerated atherosclerosis, both indirect (less exercise) and direct (inflammation drives atherosclerosis independently)
LiverAutoimmune liver disease can coexist
NeuroCarpal tunnel, mononeuritis multiplex, peripheral neuropathy, atlantoaxial subluxation (check before intubation)
General (ISAL)Fever, lymphadenopathy, weight loss, fatigue; palmar erythema, neutrophilic dermatoses, dry mouth; coronary vasculitis and valve nodules
BloodAnemia of chronic disease (or drug-induced); Felty's (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia)
KidneyLargely spared: renal disease suggests lupus or Sjögren's

Comorbidities not directly caused by RA: osteoporosis, infections, depression (a chronic pain disease), lymphoma, amyloidosis.

ISAL: EAMs are seen less often now because RA is recognized and treated earlier; the commoner ones are fatigue, subcutaneous nodules, sicca, pleural effusions, ILD and carpal tunnel.

Measuring disease activity

Serology doesn't track activity. What does: swollen and tender joint counts, validated composite scores (DAS28, CDAI, SDAI), the patient's global assessment, ESR/CRP, function (HAQ) and imaging.

X-ray of RA hands

Soft-tissue swelling (earliest) → periarticular osteopenia → uniform joint-space narrowing → marginal erosions (at the bare area where the synovium doubles over) → subluxation, ulnar deviation, swan-neck/boutonnière, carpal collapse. No osteophytes, DIPs spared. Marginal erosion = RA; central erosion = erosive OA. Films may be normal early; US/MRI are more sensitive.

  • Mechanism of erosion: neutrophils and Th17 cells activate osteoclasts.
  • Erosion vs subchondral cyst: an erosion is the surface eaten away; a cyst sits below the surface and doesn't touch it.
  • Judging osteopenia: at the midshaft the two cortices should add up to about half (at least a third) of the bone's width. Periarticular osteopenia looks like a dark lens at the bone ends.
  • Carpal collapse leaves a fixed wrist (carpal height shortens, no joint space). Orthopedic wrist fusion often reduces function a little (tutor).

Bridging and referral

Detailed urgent referral (duration, joints, stiffness, EAMs, antibodies, suspected diagnosis). While waiting: non-pharmacologic (exercise is safe, PT/OT, splints, heat or ice, Arthritis Society self-referral) and pharmacologic (full-dose NSAID e.g. naproxen 500 mg BID; intra-articular steroid for a few joints; low-dose prednisone ~10 mg, not 50). Family medicine doesn't start DMARDs. Colchicine has no role in RA.

  • Family doctors typically inject knees and shoulders; rheumatology does wrists and small joints.
  • Prednisone may make the diagnosis "a little trickier", but "I'm not in the business of making people suffer": if the patient needs treatment, treat, then taper and re-look (tutor).
  • Toronto reality: a rheumatologist won't see her in three weeks; it will take a couple of months, so bridging matters.

Starting a DMARD: counselling a hesitant patient

  • Open with autonomy: "You're the one who gets to decide. I'm not going to put anything into your body you haven't agreed to." A "you just need to take it" approach makes people refuse.
  • Patients often weigh "the wrong denominator": not treating has its own consequences (joint damage, uncontrolled inflammation, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease), so counsel both columns. "If you don't change anything, nothing changes."
  • The "you're putting me on chemo" worry: methotrexate for RA is a much lower dose than chemotherapy (the tutor said "about a quarter"; in practice 7.5–25 mg once weekly is far lower than oncology doses).
  • Patients may still decline ("you are allowed to make bad choices"). Keep seeing them; rising disease activity, time and family often change minds.

How Alex's treatment escalated

Naproxen 500 mg BID + free PT/OT (Arthritis Society self-referral) → methotrexate 25 mg PO weekly + folic acid, keeping naproxen while MTX takes effect → at 3 months wrists/MCPs/PIPs still active: add leflunomide 20 mg daily → 3 months later switch to an anti-TNF → hand synovitis resolves. The order follows Ontario funding (a biologic needs MTX + leflunomide to have failed for ≥3 months). Caveat: the case starts two teratogens in a 33-year-old without establishing her family plans; the tutor "would never start methotrexate on a patient who's wishing to have more children" (HCQ first).

Living with RA (objective MSK0300)

The non-medical side of chronic disease: collaborative care, advocacy, disability and work accommodation (Alex has missed work), self-image and self-efficacy, family dynamics (a two-year-old at home), financial stress and the cost of and access to drugs (drug coverage through work; biologic funding rules), and wait times. The patient's functional goals shape the treatment target.

A year later: the hot knee on a biologic

Septic until proven otherwise
Fever + single red, hot, swollen knee, disease otherwise controlled, on an anti-TNF → urgent arthrocentesis (cell count, Gram stain/culture, crystals; AFB/fungal if at risk) + blood cultures, hold the biologic, treat. Biologics raise infection risk (including TB) and blunt fever. A synovial WBC <50,000 doesn't exclude sepsis in the immunosuppressed, crystals and infection can coexist, and septic arthritis carries higher mortality in RA (CBL prep). Outcome (tutor): admitted; inflammatory fluid, no crystals, grew MSSA; antibiotics, biologic stopped, restart decided later.
RA = symmetric small-joint synovitis >6 weeks; >3 months argues against parvovirus (6–8 weeks). Anti-CCP most specific; RF/CCP predict course, not activity. ANA negative excludes SLE. ACR/EULAR ≥6 (classification, not diagnosis). EAMs everywhere except the kidney. Marginal erosions, osteopenia, no osteophytes. Hot joint on a biologic = aspirate for sepsis.

guides.title: Week 38 · 10 Pharmacotherapy of Rheumatic Diseases
guides.html:
SLM01 · Drugs

Pharmacotherapy of Rheumatic Diseases

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, conventional and targeted DMARDs, biologics and gout drugs: uses, mechanisms, toxicities and monitoring.

NSAIDs

Uses: acute crystal arthritis; inflammatory polyarthritis before definitive therapy; analgesia in non-inflammatory arthritis (after acetaminophen); adjunct to DMARDs; first-line for axial SpA.

Mechanism: inhibit COX (arachidonic acid → prostaglandins). COX-1 (platelets, endothelium, stomach, kidney) keeps gastric mucosa, renal function and hemostasis normal; COX-2 is induced by inflammation. Most NSAIDs are non-selective; coxibs selectively block COX-2 (only one remains marketed; others were withdrawn for CV toxicity). NSAIDs don't block leukotrienes.

SystemToxicity
GIDyspepsia → ulcers (endoscopic lesions in 20–40% within 3 months), bleeding, perforation, stricture (bowel obstruction). Ulcers may be asymptomatic, especially more distally; bleeding can be slow and subclinical (anemia, fatigue) or acute. Risk: prior GI event, age ≥60, multiple/high-dose/prolonged NSAIDs, anticoagulants, glucocorticoids, ± SSRIs/bisphosphonates. Protect with PPI or misoprostol. Dyspepsia on one NSAID may be tolerated on another; COX-2 selective drugs may carry lower gastroduodenal risk but can still cause GI intolerance in older patients. Treatment of NSAID injury: stop the NSAID.
RenalProstaglandins regulate Na/water reabsorption (thick ascending limb, collecting duct), so NSAIDs cause Na/water retention (edema, CHF), hyperkalemia, HTN, AKI/CKD, especially with ACEi/ARB/diuretics/aminoglycosides
CVRaised MI, stroke, AF and CV death with all NSAIDs, especially at high doses and with chronic use; also heart failure and HTN. Naproxen doesn't appear to share the same high-dose risk; diclofenac may have the highest. Risk may relate partly to COX-2 selectivity (less prostacyclin, PGI2, without matching inhibition of platelet thromboxane A2)
HemeAntiplatelet (COX-1). Hold ≥3 days before surgery (ASA: 1 week, irreversible). Avoid with thrombocytopenia or platelet defects. Ibuprofen may blunt ASA cardioprotection, and an NSAID is not a substitute for ASA: low-dose ASA may need to continue, with added GI risk.
OtherTransaminases; CNS effects (psychosis and cognitive impairment; headache and depersonalization with indomethacin, especially in the elderly); bronchospasm, rash, anaphylaxis; avoid after 30 weeks' gestation (ductus closure)

Monitor renal function, liver enzymes, CBC and BP in chronic users.

Glucocorticoids

First-line for most SARDs, systemic vasculitis, GCA and PMR; adjunct in RA; alternative to NSAIDs in crystal arthritis; intra-articular injection. Mechanisms: genomic (GC-receptor homodimer on DNA), indirect genomic (blocking NF-κB), non-genomic (membrane-associated receptors and second messengers), plus a non-specific membrane effect at high doses. Effects: they block leukocyte access to inflamed tissue and suppress cytokine and prostaglandin production.

Preparations: prednisone (most common oral); methylprednisolone and hydrocortisone IV; methylprednisolone acetate (Depo-Medrol) intra-articular.

Equivalents: prednisone 5 mg = methylprednisolone 4 mg = hydrocortisone 20 mg. Low ≤15 mg, medium 20–40 mg, high 40–60+ mg prednisone; IV pulses for life-threatening disease. Use the lowest effective dose, plan an end point, avoid a "shotgun" approach before a diagnosis. An intra-articular injection gives only local side effects; systemic side effects depend on duration, so a short oral course is reasonable when many joints are involved.

System (ISAL body map)Systemic glucocorticoid side effects
EyeCataract, glaucoma, blurred vision
PsychiatricSleep and mood disturbance, psychosis
Cardiovascular / renalHypertension, raised lipoproteins; hypokalemia, edema
GIGastritis, peptic ulcer
EndocrineDiabetes/hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression
MSKOsteoporosis, avascular necrosis, myopathy
Fat / skinWeight gain, Cushingoid redistribution; striae, acne, hirsutism
ImmuneImmunosuppression, lymphocytopenia, neutrophilia

SARD immunosuppressants

Steroids acutely, then steroid-sparing agents: methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide; biologics (belimumab in SLE, rituximab in vasculitis). Shared toxicities: infection, marrow suppression, malignancy, ± liver/GI. Hydroxychloroquine: minimally immunosuppressive, for mild SLE (skin, joints, fatigue); reduces flares and CV risk; retinal toxicity needs regular eye exams (visual fields and other special tests).

Rheumatoid arthritis

  • What a DMARD is: a drug that slows or halts structural joint damage. NSAIDs and steroids relieve symptoms while erosion continues, and the damage is irreversible, hence treat early.
  • Treat early (within ~3 months), treat to target (low disease activity or remission).
  • Start a single csDMARD, ideally methotrexate. The 2015 ACR algorithm (SLM01): early DMARD-naive RA → DMARD monotherapy; if moderate/high activity persists, the options are combination csDMARDs, a TNF inhibitor ± MTX, or a non-TNF biologic ± MTX (parallel options, not strict steps). Changes can be driven by side effects as well as lack of efficacy. (Ontario funding usually requires failing MTX + leflunomide ≥3 months before a biologic.)
  • HCQ: SLM01 says it doesn't prevent erosions, so it isn't considered truly disease-modifying and is used for very early/mild disease. The CBL tutor counts it among the four csDMARDs she uses in RA, and would choose it first line if the patient wants more children soon (she would occasionally start methotrexate if children are ~5 years off: "a gamble").
  • DMARDs take months (methotrexate: 6–12 weeks, so set expectations), so bridge with NSAIDs and low-dose glucocorticoid (including intra-articular).
  • Duration: potentially indefinite. After ~18–24 months of complete remission a taper can be tried as a shared decision; RF/anti-CCP-positive patients more often stay on because they flare more. Biologics are tapered by lengthening the dosing interval.
csDMARDKey toxicities
MethotrexateLiver, GI, marrow, oral ulcers; pneumonitis (rare); teratogenic and an abortifacient at higher doses. Once weekly + folic acid daily except MTX day. Avoid TMP-SMX. Limit alcohol. Switch to subcutaneous for GI intolerance; "MTX fog" the day after dosing; dose-adjust in renal impairment (renally cleared), but renal toxicity is not expected at low RA doses, so hepatic toxicity is what routine bloodwork targets (WFQ Q9); inactivated vaccines are fine (avoid live).
LeflunomideLiver, GI, marrow; teratogenic
SulfasalazineGI, hypersensitivity (skin, CBC, liver); pregnancy-compatible
Contraception on methotrexate (CBL)
Be specific or patients won't do it: an IUD is favoured; Depo-Provera is out of favour; otherwise two methods (e.g. OCP + condoms), following guidelines.

Bloodwork every 1–3 months (CBL tutor: monthly at the start, then every 3 months). Pregnancy-compatible: HCQ, sulfasalazine, certolizumab. Can't use: methotrexate, leflunomide.

Biologics and targeted synthetics

  • Anti-TNF-α (etanercept, adalimumab), anti-IL-6R (tocilizumab), anti-CD20 (rituximab); small-molecule JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, oral). Scope (ISAL): you don't need the biologic/tsDMARD names or the differences between drug families at this level. Biologics are large proteins given IV or subcutaneously. Biosimilars are highly similar but not identical to the originator, with no clinically meaningful differences in safety or effectiveness, and are more cost-effective. Access in Ontario: private plans, Trillium Drug Program, Exceptional Access Program.
  • Shared risks: infection (opportunistic, TB and hepatitis B reactivation: screen CXR/TB test and HBV serology first), stop for intercurrent infection and peri-operatively, no live vaccines (vaccinate beforehand), injection/infusion reactions; anti-TNF: non-melanoma skin cancer.

Spondyloarthritis

All SpA patients: education, exercise, physiotherapy, analgesia (some need surgery). Peripheral SpA only: csDMARDs (e.g. methotrexate), then a biologic/tsDMARD, much like RA. Any axial disease: NSAIDs first, then straight to biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-17). In axial SpA NSAIDs count as disease-modifying, and csDMARDs don't work (ISAL).

Gout drugs

DrugRole and cautions
ColchicineAcute flare only early (12–36 h); disrupts neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis. Diarrhea, marrow and muscle toxicity; poorly cleared in elderly and renal disease. Also low-dose prophylaxis.
AllopurinolXanthine oxidase inhibitor; titrate to urate <360 µmol/L, continue indefinitely. Can trigger flares at the start (cover 3–6 months after target), azathioprine interaction, rare severe hypersensitivity.
FebuxostatXO inhibitor only if allopurinol isn't tolerated
LosartanUricosuric ARB, useful when an antihypertensive is needed. SGLT2i also lower urate.
Other urate-lowering mechanismsIncrease excretion: uricosurics such as probenecid and sulfinpyrazone (Lec01: no longer available in Canada; SLM01 names only losartan and says others are "not widely available in Canada"). Convert urate to soluble allantoin: rasburicase (urate oxidase; not routinely available). Only allopurinol and febuxostat are indicated for gout in Canada (Lec01).

Fibromyalgia

Non-drug measures first; duloxetine (SNRI) or pregabalin. Not NSAIDs or opioids.

NSAIDs: GI (PPI), kidney (hyperkalemia, AKI, especially with ACEi/diuretics), CV; avoid in CKD/CHF and late pregnancy. Pred 5 = MP 4 = HC 20. MTX: weekly, folate, liver/marrow/ulcers, teratogen. Biologics: screen TB + HBV, no live vaccines. Gout: colchicine early; allopurinol to <360 with flare cover.
