guides.html:
Anatomy

Upper Limb I: Vessels, Shoulder, Axilla & Brachial Plexus

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The arterial and venous routes down the limb, the four shoulder-complex joints, the shoulder muscles and rotator cuff, the axilla, and the brachial plexus.

Arteries and veins

VesselCourse and key branches
Subclavian → axillaryAxillary artery gives the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries around the surgical neck (shoulder supply)
BrachialBegins at the lower border of teres major; superficial, anterior to triceps and brachialis (palpable). Branch: profunda brachii, which runs with the radial nerve along the radial groove on the posterior humerus
UlnarDeep to pronator teres; gives the common interosseous → anterior and posterior interosseous
RadialDeep to brachioradialis; winds around the lateral wrist through the anatomical snuff box
HandSuperficial and deep palmar arches
Superficial veinsDorsal venous network → cephalic (lateral) and basilic (medial), joined by the median cubital vein in the cubital fossa (venipuncture). The basilic goes deep in the arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein; the cephalic goes deep near the clavicle (clavipectoral triangle) to join the axillary vein (the lecturer said subclavian)

The shoulder complex

Scapular movements (elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, upward rotation for abduction, downward rotation for adduction) come from the combined sternoclavicular + acromioclavicular joints.

JointKey anatomyClinical
SternoclavicularSaddle-type synovial joint with an articular disc; SC, interclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments; moves with every arm elevationThe only bony link of the limb to the axial skeleton
AcromioclavicularSmall plane synovial joint with very little movement; the coracoclavicular ligament is the main stabilizerSeparated shoulder = AC joint disruption (clavicle rides up; GH intact)
GlenohumeralBall and socket; humeral head + shallow glenoid deepened by the glenoid labrum (complete fibrocartilage ring). Static: glenohumeral (sup/mid/inf) and coracohumeral ligaments. Dynamic: rotator cuff. Coracoacromial arch blocks superior dislocation. Subacromial bursa; the long head of biceps runs through the jointDislocated shoulder = GH. Most mobile, least stable joint
Why the shoulder dislocates inferiorly
The humeral head sits only about one-third of a sphere in the glenoid (the hip holds about two-thirds), which buys mobility at the cost of stability. Inferiorly there is no bone and no rotator cuff muscle, so most dislocations go down first and are then pulled to the front or back.

Bursae: the subacromial bursa lies between deltoid and supraspinatus and can become inflamed with a lot of rubbing; the subtendinous bursa of subscapularis is the other one to know. The lecturer linked these bursae to frozen shoulder; strictly, frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is inflammation and fibrosis of the GH capsule, while bursal inflammation fits subacromial bursitis/impingement.

Shoulder muscles

MuscleAction (GH)Nerve
Deltoid (clavicle, acromion, scapular spine → deltoid tuberosity)All fibres abduct; anterior flexes, posterior extendsAxillary
Pectoralis majorClavicular head flexes; sternocostal head adducts and internally rotatesMedial and lateral pectoral
Latissimus dorsiThe major shoulder extensor; adducts; internally rotates (it wraps to the front of the humerus)Thoracodorsal
Teres majorExtends, adducts, internally rotatesLower subscapular

"Two majors and a lady in between": pec major, latissimus ("lady") and teres major all insert at the intertubercular sulcus, and all three internally rotate.

Rotator cuff: "SITS"

MuscleInsertionActionNerve
SupraspinatusGreater tubercleInitiates abduction (first ~15°); passes under the coracoacromial arch (impingement)Suprascapular
InfraspinatusGreater tubercleExternal rotationSuprascapular
Teres minorGreater tubercleExternal rotationAxillary
SubscapularisLesser tubercleInternal rotationUpper and lower subscapular

"SItS" is written with a lowercase t as a reminder: it is teres minor, not teres major. Supraspinatus is the only cuff muscle that does no rotation. With supraspinatus or suprascapular-nerve loss, patients can still abduct by a trick: flex slightly first, then abduct, because deltoid runs on a different nerve (axillary) (Lec03).

The axilla

A pyramidal passageway for neurovascular structures. Apex: clavicle, 1st rib, scapula. Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor. Posterior wall: subscapularis (with teres major, latissimus dorsi). Medial wall: thoracic wall and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Base: skin and subcutaneous tissue of the armpit. Contents: axillary artery and vein, lymphatics/nodes, fat, brachial plexus (in the axillary sheath).

Brachial plexus (C5–T1 anterior rami)

Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches ("Really Tired? Drink Coffee Black"). Trunks: upper (C5–6), middle (C7), lower (C8–T1). Each splits into anterior and posterior divisions. Cords are named by their relation to the axillary artery: lateral, medial, posterior (formed from all three posterior divisions). You won't be asked to draw it, but you must know the root values of the 5 terminal branches; the small collateral branches (pectoral, subscapular, thoracodorsal, suprascapular) don't need root values. A plexus gives redundancy: one lesion may spare part of a muscle's supply.

  • The rami emerge between the anterior and middle scalenes; impingement there can cause symptoms all the way down to the fingers.
  • The "M": lateral cord → musculocutaneous; medial cord → ulnar; a branch from each forms the median nerve.
  • The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis. The ulnar nerve supplies nothing in the arm.
Terminal branchCordRootsSupplies
MusculocutaneousLateralC5–C7Anterior arm (flexors)
MedianLateral + medialC5–C6, C8–T1 per lecture (standard texts: C5/6–T1, incl. C7 via lateral cord)Most forearm flexors, thenar muscles
UlnarMedialC8–T1FCU, medial ½ FDP, most intrinsic hand muscles
AxillaryPosteriorC5–C6Deltoid, teres minor
RadialPosteriorC5–T1Posterior arm and forearm (extensors)

Skin supply (Lec03 slide 20)

NerveSkin
AxillaryOver the deltoid
RadialPosterior arm and forearm; a strip of lateral arm; dorsum of the lateral hand (dorsal thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger) sparing the fingertips, via the superficial branch of the radial n.
MusculocutaneousLateral forearm
MedianLateral palm and lateral 3½ digits, including the dorsal fingertips
UlnarMedial hand, palmar and dorsal: medial 1½ digits
T1 / T2Medial forearm (T1) and medial arm (T2): not from the 5 terminal branches
Fracture → nerve at risk
Mid-shaft humerus fracture → radial nerve (and profunda brachii) in the radial groove, lying right on bone. Surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve (and posterior circumflex humeral artery). Median and ulnar nerves are cushioned by muscle.
Axillary → brachial (at teres major) → radial + ulnar. Separated = AC; dislocated = GH. SITS: supra (initiates abduction), infra + teres minor (ER), subscapularis (IR, lesser tubercle); suprascapular nerve for supra/infra, axillary for teres minor and deltoid. Mid-shaft humerus = radial nerve; surgical neck = axillary nerve.

guides.title: Week 38 · 12 Upper Limb II: Elbow, Forearm, Wrist & Hand
guides.html:
Anatomy

Upper Limb II: Elbow, Forearm, Wrist & Hand

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Elbow and wrist joints, carpal bones, the two-compartment arm and forearm with their nerves and exceptions, and the cubital fossa, carpal tunnel and snuff box.

Elbow

  • Compound hinge synovial joint: humeroulnar (trochlea + trochlear notch) and humeroradial (capitulum + radial head). The proximal radioulnar joint shares the capsule.
  • Stability: ulnar and radial collateral ligaments; the anular ligament wraps the radial head.
  • Fat pads lie outside the synovial membrane and are easily displaced by an effusion or inflammation, which changes what you see on POCUS and X-ray (the sail sign).
  • Children: ossification is incomplete until the teens. At 4 y only the capitulum and radial head are marked; by 13 y all six are (mnemonic CRITOE: Capitulum, Radial head, Internal/medial epicondyle, Trochlea, Olecranon, External/lateral epicondyle). So in toddlers the anular ligament does most of the work of holding the radial head, and it can slip when a child is lifted or swung by the hands ("nursemaid's elbow": a "pop", persistent crying). Reduce with supination/pronation; reaching out to grab something with that arm shows function is back (Lec03).

Pronation and supination

Proximal + distal radioulnar joints: only the radius rotates around a fixed ulna, so only muscles attaching to the radius can pronate or supinate. Supinators: biceps brachii (radial tuberosity) and supinator. Pronators: pronator teres and pronator quadratus. ("Supine: you can hold a bowl of soup.")

Wrist and hand

  • Carpals (lateral to medial, starting at the thumb). Proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate ("Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle"; trapezium is by the thumb).
  • Wrist (radiocarpal): condyloid synovial. Distal radius + articular disc over the ulna, against scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum (not pisiform, which sits on the triquetrum). Flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation. The lecture places the distal radioulnar joint within the capsule (standard texts note the articular disc separates the two cavities).
  • CMC1 = saddle (its shape allows opposition); CMC2–5 = plane. MCP = condyloid. IP = hinge.
  • Finger abduction and adduction at the MCPs are measured from the middle finger as the midline (these tests matter in the neuro exam).

Two fascial compartments

Deep fascia, intermuscular septa and the interosseous membrane divide the arm and forearm into anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) compartments (the thigh and leg have three).

RegionAnteriorPosterior
ArmBiceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis. Musculocutaneous n. Biceps: long head through the glenohumeral joint, short head from the coracoid; inserts on the radial tuberosity, so it flexes and supinates. Brachialis inserts on the ulna (pure elbow flexor). Coracobrachialis: coracoid to humerus, crosses only the shoulder and flexes the shoulderTriceps brachii (ulna/olecranon): extensor, no pronation/supination. Radial n.
ForearmWrist and digit flexors + pronators. Common flexor origin: medial epicondyle. Superficial: pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FCU; intermediate: FDS; deep: FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus. Median n. except FCU and medial ½ FDP (ulnar)Wrist and digit extensors. Common extensor origin: lateral epicondyle. Radial n. / posterior interosseous n. Exceptions: brachioradialis (flexes the elbow, strongest in the neutral/thumbs-up position, the "drinking muscle"; it doesn't cross the wrist, so it can't extend it, and it is grouped with the extensors only because of its radial innervation) and supinator (the deep branch of the radial n. passes through it). The PIN is simply the deep branch of the radial n.; you don't need to know which muscles radial vs PIN supplies

Posterior forearm muscles (Lec03 slide 32)

LayerMuscles
SuperficialBrachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB, ECU (the primary wrist extensors), extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi
DeepSupinator, APL, EPB, EPL (thumb), extensor indicis

Extensor digitorum flattens over each digit into the extensor hood, and many of the small intrinsic muscles of the hand attach into that hood.

Flexor details

  • FDS splits "like a snake's tongue" so the FDP tendon can pass through to the distal phalanx. FDP serves digits 2–5; FPL the thumb.
  • Palmaris longus is vestigial and absent in some people. It passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum; oppose thumb to little finger and flex the wrist to see its tendon.
  • The long flexor tendons run in synovial sheaths that can become inflamed (tenosynovitis).

Hand muscles

About 18 intrinsic hand muscles, taught in groups; names aren't required, but all 8 carpal names and positions are (Lec03). Thenar muscles: median n. Hypothenar and adductor pollicis: ulnar n. The ulnar nerve supplies most intrinsic hand muscles (lesions give a characteristic claw hand).

Clinically important regions

RegionBoundariesContents
Cubital fossaSuperior: line between the epicondyles. Medial: pronator teres. Lateral: brachioradialis. Roof: fascia + bicipital aponeurosisLateral to medial: (radial n., deep), biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve. Median cubital vein superficially. The radial nerve reaches the forearm under brachioradialis; the ulnar nerve is not in the fossa: it runs behind the medial epicondyle just under the skin (the "funny bone")
Carpal tunnelFloor: carpal bones. Roof: flexor retinaculum4 FDS + 4 FDP + FPL tendons + median nerve. Not in the tunnel: FCR and FCU (the wrist flexors); palmaris longus runs over the retinaculum. The palmar cutaneous branch passes over the retinaculum, so palm sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome
Anatomical snuff boxRadial side: APL + EPB tendons. Ulnar side: EPL. Floor: scaphoid + trapeziumRadial artery, cephalic vein, superficial branch of radial nerve
Clinical pearls
Snuff-box tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand = scaphoid injury until proven otherwise (fractures can have a normal first X-ray and risk avascular necrosis). Carpal tunnel syndrome: thumb/radial-digit tingling and thenar weakness with a spared palm. A median lesion higher up (arm or neck) would also lose palm sensation and impair thumb and finger flexion. Trigger finger: catching/locking of a finger with a palpable nodule at the palmar MCP = flexor digitorum superficialis tendon (lecture answer); the nodule catches on the A1 pulley.
Only the radius moves in pronation/supination: biceps + supinator supinate. Anterior compartments = flexors (musculocutaneous arm, median forearm except FCU + ½ FDP = ulnar); posterior = extensors (radial), exceptions brachioradialis and supinator. Cubital fossa: TAN (tendon, artery, nerve) lateral to medial. Carpal tunnel: 9 tendons + median nerve. Snuff box: radial artery over scaphoid.

guides.title: Week 38 · 13 Clinical Skills I: Rheumatology History & Joint Exam
guides.html:
CS2 · Rheum 1 & 2

Clinical Skills I: Rheumatology History & Joint Exam

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

Everything from the Rheum 1 and 2 sessions: how to take and describe a joint history, the exam principles, the full shoulder, wrist/hand and knee exams with every maneuver, GALS, and the picture cases.

The MSK clinical skills block

SessionContent
Rheum 1Rheumatologic history and exam principles; shoulder, wrist and hand exams
Rheum 2Inspection as a diagnostic tool; knee exam; GALS screen
Ortho hip / Ortho backHip exam; mechanical low back pain (see the next guide)

Joint history: the seven principles

  1. Articular, periarticular or non-articular? Articular pain runs through the joint's whole range of motion. Periarticular pain (tendon, bursa, ligament, muscle) appears only in the direction that loads the painful structure. Non-articular pain is unrelated to movement. Burning, tingling, crawling or pins and needles point to neuropathic pain, not arthritis.
  2. How many joints? Mono = 1, oligo = 2–4, poly = 5 or more (some use 4).
  3. Characteristics: onset, duration (acute vs chronic: chronic arthritis = >6 weeks), course, severity.
  4. Nature: inflammatory (swelling, warmth, erythema, stiffness with immobility, morning stiffness >30 min), non-inflammatory (little swelling, cool, pain worse with use, brief stiffness) or damage (deformity, crepitus).
  5. Distribution: large vs small (and "medium": wrists, ankles), upper vs lower, symmetric vs asymmetric, axial vs peripheral (axial: OA, axial SpA such as ankylosing spondylitis; peripheral: peripheral SpA such as psoriatic arthritis). Symmetric means the same joint groups on both sides (e.g. MCPs on both hands), not necessarily identical joints. SI pain is felt in the low back/buttock; hip pain is felt in the groin.
  6. Function: ADLs/IADLs, work, leisure and social life (e.g. can't sit through the drive to see family).
  7. Associated features: constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss), ILD (RA), cardiac (lupus), uveitis, IBD, psoriasis. Then a full PMH, medications, allergies, family and social history.

Asking about each symptom

SymptomHow to ask / what it means
Stiffness"When you wake up, how long until your joints loosen up to the best they'll be all day?" 30–60 min or more = inflammatory; <30 min = OA. Gelling: stiff after ≥1 h of immobility (getting up after a nap or a long sit). Fibromyalgia patients also report lots of stiffness, so stiffness alone doesn't prove inflammation
SwellingAsk about warmth and redness; characterize it: firm (bony), boggy/bouncy (synovitis) or fluid-like (effusion)
WeaknessSudden and one-sided: stroke. Gradual over weeks to months: inflammatory myositis. Worse with repeated use: myasthenia gravis
FatigueAn inclination to rest when pain and weakness aren't the limiting factors (waking unrefreshed). Prominent in inflammatory arthritis, and also driven by anxiety and depression
CrepitusTutor's teaching: fine crepitus = cartilage damage (e.g. erosive inflammatory arthritis); coarse = bone on bone (OA). Painless pops and cracks are benign
Pain scalePain is subjective; anchor 10 as the worst pain imaginable. Pain described as excruciating while function is preserved suggests catastrophizing or psychosocial amplification

Start open-ended ("tell me about it") and let the patient tell the story, then fill gaps: constant vs movement-related, which movements, time of day, trajectory, what helps or worsens it. When asking about Raynaud's, show a picture: many people over-report it (Lec02).

Exam principles

  • Expose both sides; compare with the normal side (examine it first so the patient knows what normal feels like); examine the joint above and below; watch gait for back and lower-limb problems; watch the patient's face for pain.
  • Look → Feel → Move → Special tests. Be systematic and tell the examiner your order (e.g. inspect, palpate and move the arms, then the same for the legs). Rheumatologists often go top to bottom: TMJ, sternoclavicular/manubriosternal, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hands.
  • Palpation pressure: enough to blanch your own thumbnail (about 4 kg/cm²). Tenderness is a sign you elicit on palpation; pain is the symptom the patient reports.
  • Stress pain: pain when the joint is taken gently just beyond (or at the end of) its normal range; indicates inflammatory articular disease.
  • Synovitis feels like a grape (soft, boggy, bouncy); OA bony enlargement feels like a chocolate-covered almond (hard). Rheumatologists record a swollen joint count and a tender joint count separately. The swollen count correlates better with disease progression, but newer studies show tenderness without swelling also predicts damage, so do the 4-point exam even when nothing looks swollen.
  • Recording (CBL): go proximal to distal (wrists → MCPs → PIPs → DIPs) on a homunculus: filled circle = swollen, open circle = tender without swelling (some legends use X for tender).
  • Active ROM needs intact joint, muscle, tendon and nerve. If active range is full, symmetric and painless, passive testing isn't needed. Articular disease hurts on active and passive movement; periarticular disease hurts on active but not passive movement.
  • Deformity = malalignment of two articulating bones. Dislocation = complete loss of contact; subluxation = partial; fixed flexion deformity; valgus = distal bone deviates away from the midline (knock-knees; "valgus forms an L"), varus = toward the midline (bow legs). Swelling around a joint may be soft tissue, fluid, tendon or bone.
LookFeelMove
PeriarticularFocal swelling/redness at a bursa, tendon or insertionFocal tendernessPain only in certain directions; less pain passively
Articular inflammationDiffuse joint swelling, rednessWarm; joint-line tenderness; stress pain; effusionPain through active and passive range
Articular damageDeformityJoint-line tendernessCrepitus; reduced active and passive range; instability

Shoulder exam

Prep: wash hands, introduce and explain; expose both shoulders (gown lowered under the axillae, chest covered).

  • Inspect: asymmetry; masses, scars, bruises (skin bleeding by size: petechiae small → purpura medium → ecchymosis large, the medical term for a bruise); erythema; effusion (a pad in front of the shoulder, loss of the normal anterior contour: RA or septic arthritis); muscle atrophy (chronic problem, disuse as in frozen shoulder; the humeral head looks prominent); bony changes (squaring, prominent SC joint or clavicle); biceps rupture ("Popeye" ball of tissue mid-humerus on flexing).
  • Palpate (watch the face): SC joint → length of clavicle (discontinuity) → AC joint (OA affects it even more than the GH joint; it can be injected by landmark) → subacromial space (bursa) → bicipital groove → cuff insertions (greater and lesser tuberosities) → GH crepitus (hand on top of the shoulder while passively flexing and circumducting the arm).
  • Active ROM (note limits, asymmetry, pain): flexion ("raise straight arms in front and overhead"), extension ("behind you"), abduction ("out to the side and overhead"), adduction ("cross the straight arm in front"), internal rotation ("hand behind your back to your shoulder blade"; record the highest spinous process reached), external rotation ("hand behind your head, as if brushing your hair").
  • Passive ROM (only if active is limited): one hand on the scapula to stop it moving; support the arm flexed at the elbow and move through flexion, extension, abduction and adduction; test IR/ER either with the arm abducted to 90° or with the elbow tucked at the side (forearm toward the abdomen = IR; out to ~45° = ER).
Special testHowTests
Resisted external rotationElbow tucked at the waist; examiner rotates the forearm outward, then pushes it back toward neutral as the patient resistsInfraspinatus + teres minor
Resisted internal rotationElbow tucked; forearm rotated inward, examiner pulls outward as the patient resistsSubscapularis
Empty canArms at 45° (shoulder level in the scapular plane), thumbs pointing down; press down as the patient resistsSupraspinatus
Neer'sStand behind/beside; stabilize the shoulder; with the arm internally rotated (thumb down), passively forward-flex it overhead; watch for painSubacromial impingement (greater tuberosity jammed under the anteroinferior acromion)

Inflammation of the coracoacromial ligament or subacromial bursitis causes impingement; a subacromial steroid injection gives fast relief when abduction is limited.

Wrist and hand exam

Prep: both hands and wrists exposed; hands held unsupported with elbows flexed to 90°. Palpate one hand at a time.

  • Inspect dorsal and palmar surfaces: masses, nodules, scars, cuts, bruising; erythema (may look like hyperpigmentation in darker skin); swelling; thenar/hypothenar atrophy (thenar flattening in carpal tunnel syndrome); flexor tendon sheath swelling; thickened, shiny or tight skin; fingertip pitting/scarring.
  • Deformities: swan neck (PIP hyperextension + DIP flexion) and boutonnière (PIP flexion + DIP hyperextension) in RA; ulnar deviation with MCP subluxation (RA); fusiform (spindle) PIP swelling (synovitis); Heberden's nodes at the DIPs ("Heberden, closer to heaven") and Bouchard's nodes at the PIPs (OA); squaring of the first CMC (OA); dactylitis (sausage digit: PsA/SpA); tophi (gout).
  • Effusions: wrist; MCP: loss of the "valleys" between the knuckles when a fist is made; PIP/DIP: loss of skin creases and fusiform swelling.
  • Nails: pitting, onycholysis (nail lifting off the bed), oil-drop spots (yellow discoloration from serum collecting around subungual hyperkeratosis), ridges and subungual hyperkeratosis (psoriasis; the tutor called the ridges "Beau's lines", but Beau's lines are transverse grooves from temporary nail-growth arrest in any systemic illness, not a psoriatic sign); periungual erythema, nailfold capillary dilatation and micro-hemorrhages (lupus, systemic sclerosis, myositis); infarcts. Note nail polish if present.
PalpateTechnique
True radiocarpal jointTrace the 3rd metacarpal proximally to its base; press with one thumb at the dorsal indentation while feeling for fluid with the other. You should feel a groove; synovitis makes it bouncy and the groove disappears
MCP squeezeScreen: gently squeeze across the MCPs (include the thumb). Pain means go joint by joint
MCPsFlex the MCPs slightly; thumbs just distal to each MCP head at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions; press with one and feel fluid move against the other
PIPs and DIPsFour-point technique: thumb and index of one hand on the sides, thumb and index of the other on top and bottom; press one pair, feel fluid against the other, then reverse
First CMCIn the anatomical snuff box / base of the thumb (groove over the joint): a common OA site
  • Active ROM: wrist flexion (~90°, more than extension), extension, radial and ulnar deviation (ulnar greater), pronation, supination; make a fist and open the fingers (MCP/PIP/DIP flexion and extension).
  • Passive ROM + stress (only if active is limited): grip the hand as if shaking it, sliding proximally to avoid squeezing the fingers; move the wrist through each direction with slight stress at end range. MCPs: flex/extend each via the proximal phalanx. PIPs: flex the fingertip to the palm, or gently hyperextend. DIPs: flex the fingertip toward the base of the metacarpals, or gently hyperextend.
  • Function: power grip ("squeeze my fingers; don't let me pull away"); precision (touch each fingertip to the thumb).
  • Extras shown in the session: Finkelstein's (as demonstrated, strictly the Eichhoff variant: thumb tucked in a fist, then ulnar deviation: pain over the radial styloid = De Quervain's tenosynovitis of APL/EPB); Tinel's (tap over the carpal tunnel: tingling in the median distribution); Phalen's (reverse prayer, wrists flexed for 1 min: reproduces carpal tunnel symptoms); hypermobility screen (thumb passively touches the forearm; 5th finger extends past 90°), a common arthritis mimic.
  • Carpal tunnel: conservative care (tutor): a wrist splint at night (wrists flex and extend unknowingly during sleep, inflaming the tendon sheath and compressing the median nerve), off during the day except for strenuous wrist activity; topical NSAIDs for shallow structures, rest, ice, elevation.

Knee exam

  • Standing: gait; alignment (valgus knock-knee, varus bow-leg, genu recurvatum); look behind for a Baker's cyst (soft popliteal fullness from effusion tracking posteriorly, classically with OA; the front may be empty).
  • Supine (draped so thighs are visible, groin covered): asymmetry, masses, scars, quadriceps atrophy, erythema, effusion (suprapatellar fullness, loss of the medial fossa just medial and inferior to the patella).
  • Temperature: back of the fingers above, on and below the patella, both sides. The patella should be cooler than the tissue above and below; a warmer knee suggests inflammation.
  • Joint-line tenderness: flex the knee with the foot flat; find the joint line by palpating up from the tibial tuberosity along the patellar tendon; press each side separately with the thumbs.
Effusion testTechniqueDetects
Bulge signSweep upward along the medial side to empty the medial fossa into the suprapatellar pouch; then stroke down the lateral side (below the patella) and watch the medial fossa for a returning bulge. Done medial-first because the lateral side is bulkier (IT band, vastus lateralis)Small effusion. No bulge = no effusion, or one too large to sweep
Ballottement / patellar tapCompress the suprapatellar pouch with one hand (without squeezing soft tissue); press the patella with thumb and index of the other and feel a fluid wave or the patella tapping downLarger effusion
  • ROM: active "heel to buttock, then straighten". Passive (handout): one hand on the knee (feel crepitus over the patella and both joint lines), the other grasping the heel gently to flex and extend the knee. In the GALS demo the tutor held just proximal to the ankle to avoid pressing on painful joints.
  • Ligaments: anterior drawer (knee flexed ~90°, hamstrings relaxed, stabilize the foot with your forearm or by sitting near it, grasp the upper tibia and pull forward: anterior translation = ACL); posterior drawer (same position, push back = PCL); valgus stress with the knee slightly flexed, hand on the lateral knee (medial opening = MCL); varus stress, hand on the medial knee (lateral opening = LCL).
  • While the leg is up, flex the hip and test hip internal and external rotation: groin pain points to the hip.

GALS screening exam

Use GALS to rapidly screen for an underlying or concomitant MSK disorder. Three screening questions: "Do you have pain or stiffness in your muscles, joints or back?" "Can you dress yourself completely without difficulty?" "Can you walk up and down stairs without difficulty?"

PartWhat to do and look for
GaitSymmetry and smoothness, arm swing, stride and stance width, turning. Antalgic: short stance on the painful side. Trendelenburg: weak hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus), pointing to hip pathology (WFQ Q18). Steppage: foot drop
ArmsInspect shoulders (level, muscle bulk), elbows (full extension; women have a greater normal carrying/valgus angle). "Hands behind your head, elbows out" = shoulder abduction + external rotation. Hands out palms down, then up: wrists, small joints, nails, thenar/hypothenar bulk, pronation/supination. MCP squeeze. Power grip and fingertip-to-thumb precision
LegsStanding: quads, knees, feet and toes. Supine: inspect again up close; quick effusion check (patellar tap); passive hip and knee flexion; hip IR/ER (groin or buttock pain); MTP squeeze, then individual MTPs if positive; inspect the feet
SpineFrom behind: straight spine, symmetric paraspinals, level iliac crests. From the side: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis. Loss of curves suggests muscle spasm (often secondary to pain), degeneration or fracture. Lateral neck flexion ("ear to shoulder") and lumbar flexion

Picture cases from the session

PictureDiagnosis clue
Swollen MCP2–3 and PIPs, fusiform fingers, ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation, ILDRA
Symmetric hard DIP + PIP enlargement, CMC squaringOA (Heberden/Bouchard)
Hand X-ray: DIPs, PIPs, thumb IP and first CMC involvedOA. The tutor called it the "seagull sign" and pointed to joint-line sclerosis (bone thickening); strictly, the seagull (gull-wing) sign is the central erosion + marginal osteophytes of erosive IP-joint OA
DIP disease with onycholysis, oil spots, ridges; whole-thumb swellingPsoriatic arthritis (dactylitis)
Chalky nodules, red swollen DIPTophaceous gout
Fingertips white → blue → red in the cold (the red phase is the painful one)Raynaud's (with lupus, SSc, myositis, RA, vasculitis)
Symmetric palpable purpura on the legsIgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein): IgA deposits in vessels after a systemic infection; mostly self-limiting; check the urine. Palpable purpura sits in size between petechiae and ecchymoses
Acute red, hot first MTP in a man with CKDGout (podagra)
Acute swollen knee: suprapatellar swelling, lost medial fossaAcute monoarthritis: aspirate

Physiotherapists and occupational therapists (SLM04)

  • PT: reduce pain, improve mobility and strength, prevent deformity. Exercise, education and self-management have the best evidence (plus manual therapy and electrotherapy). Direct access: patients can self-refer. PTs are also trained in cardiovascular and neurological assessment. In RA: strengthening and mobility exercises, plus secondary prevention of RA's high cardiovascular risk (prescribed physical activity, lifestyle change, smoking cessation) alongside the rheumatologist (SLM04 narration).
  • OT: function and meaningful occupation (self-care, productivity, leisure) through pain management, energy conservation, deformity correction, splinting and assistive devices. OTs tailor the assessment to the activities the patient most wants back (work, personal care, leisure such as playing an instrument), using occupation-based tasks (dressing, meal preparation, work). Direct access, but some insurers require a physician referral before they cover OT (SLM04).
  • Non-drug care works alongside drugs: in ankylosing spondylitis, biologics + physiotherapy/exercise beat biologics alone for symptoms, function and quality of life (SLM04 narration).
  • Funding in Ontario: extended health benefits, insurance/WSIB or out of pocket; OHIP through hospitals, FHTs and CHCs. OHIP community physio clinics are for those ≥65 or ≤19, recently discharged (for the admitting condition), or on ODSP/Ontario Works. Any arthritis diagnosis qualifies for the Arthritis Society's Rehabilitation and Education Program.
History: articular? how many? acute (<6 wk) or chronic? inflammatory (stiffness 30–60+ min, gelling, warmth) or mechanical? distribution? function? extra-articular? Exam: look, feel (blanch-the-nail pressure, stress pain, grape vs almond), move (active, then passive), special tests. Shoulder: ER = infraspinatus/teres minor, IR = subscapularis, empty can = supraspinatus, Neer = impingement. Hand: radiocarpal via 3rd metacarpal, MCP squeeze, 4-point PIP/DIP, nails. Knee: patella cooler, bulge = small, ballottement = large, drawers and varus/valgus.

guides.html:
CS2 · Ortho Back

Clinical Skills II: Mechanical Low Back Pain (Ortho Back)

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite

The patterns-of-pain system in full: the history questions and how to ask them, every exam maneuver and nerve-root test, the four patterns with their subsets, and the pattern-specific treatment.

Why classify by pattern

  • "Distinct patterns of reliable clinical findings are the only logical basis for back pain categorization and subsequent treatment" (Quebec Task Force, 1987). The system was designed by Dr. Hamilton Hall.
  • Classify on the pattern, not the pain's character: sharp, burning or shooting descriptions vary and don't decide the pattern. Muscle spasm is compensatory, not a pattern or a pain source.
  • >90% of primary-care back pain is mechanical (related to movement or position) from structures that usually can't be pinned down. <5% is malignancy, infection, systemic illness or major trauma; cauda equina is <1%.
  • The old pathoanatomical approach fails in the spine: the painful structure or level can't be identified, and imaging misleads. X-ray degeneration doesn't correlate with pain; as screening tools CT has ~30% and MRI ~90% false positives. Pattern-based care reduces imaging, MRI use, surgery and medication.
  • A syndrome is a consistent cluster of signs and symptoms that responds to treatment predictably (a disease with unknown etiology). Identify the pattern with a focused history and confirm it with a concordant exam. Red-flag screening accompanies pattern recognition; it doesn't precede it. Consider sinister causes when there's no clear pattern or no response to pattern-based treatment.

History: the three pattern questions

QuestionHow to ask and interpret
1. "Where is your pain the worst?"Draw a line at the inferior gluteal fold. Back-dominant = most intense in the low back, buttock, coccyx, groin or over the greater trochanters (referred pain from a spinal structure). Leg-dominant = around or below the gluteal fold into the thigh, calf, ankle or foot (radicular pain: nerve root irritation). One site always predominates. If the patient won't choose: "I have to start with one pain. If I could stop only one, which would it be?" Leg pain from the spine must change with back movement or position (unlike a knee ligament problem). If it can't be decided, assume leg-dominant (worst case). Surgeons ask this because it decides the operation: back-dominant → fusion; leg-dominant → decompression. When a root is involved in leg-dominant pain it is most commonly L5 or S1, then L4, usually from an adjacent acute disc herniation
2. "Is your pain constant or intermittent?"Two parts: (A) "Is there ever a time during the day when your pain stops, even for a moment, even though it comes back?" (B) "When it stops, is it completely gone?" "Nearly/mostly gone" = constant. Give permission to have intermittent pain, repeat the answer back to confirm, and if unsure, assume constant. Truly intermittent back-dominant pain is never spinal malignancy or active infection: a powerful reassurance. Constant pain can still be mechanical (like the first day of an ankle sprain) but prompts red-flag questions
3. "Does bending forward make your typical pain worse?"Flexion is the key aggravating movement. Interpret activities: sitting, driving, brushing teeth over the sink, putting on shoes, climbing stairs = flexion; standing, walking, leaning back, painting a ceiling = extension. We spend ~70% of the day flexed

The mandatory question

"Since the start of your current pain, has there been any change in your bladder or bowel function?" (framed this way to exclude long-standing unrelated problems).

Cauda equina syndrome: surgical emergency
The cord ends around L2; below it the nerve roots form the cauda equina. A large central disc herniation (the tutor cited the L5–S1 level as typical) compresses multiple sacral roots (S2–S4), which control the sphincters and saddle sensation:
• Urinary retention followed by insensible overflow (the bladder can't empty, then leaks "like a dripping tap")
• Fecal incontinence (unrecognized)
• Saddle (perineal) numbness
Needs immediate surgical decompression to preserve sphincter function; delay makes the loss permanent (the session cited the first 24–72 h as the window).

The other questions

  • Function: "What can't you do now that you could before, and why?" The reason should be the same pain named in Q1 and should fit the aggravating movement (e.g. can't lift boxes = flexion). If the reason is inconsistent ("my boss won't pay me"), resolve it: a clue to yellow flags. Motivation and belief that you'll recover are among the strongest prognostic factors.
  • Relieving movements/positions; previous episodes (back pain is recurrent, "like asthma": we manage rather than cure); previous treatment and whether it worked (active vs passive therapy).
  • Non-mechanical screen: "If you're under 45, do you have morning back stiffness lasting >30 min?" Inflammatory spine disease is <5% of back pain but the second most common pathology.
  • When pain is constant and non-mechanical, ask about: pain unaffected by movement or position, severe or progressive neuro deficits, unexplained weight loss, recent/ongoing infection, failure to respond to appropriate mechanical treatment within days–weeks, disproportionate night pain (unrelenting, with night sweats), constitutional symptoms, cancer in the past 5 years.

Rules: history outranks the exam; when in doubt choose the more serious option (leg-dominant, constant); give mechanical treatment a fair trial before labelling pain non-mechanical.

Physical examination

The exam verifies or refutes the history. Efficient order by position: standing → kneeling on a chair → sitting → sitting on the table → supine → prone.

  • Observe: general behaviour (filling in forms standing up suggests flexion hurts; squatting in a queue suggests extension hurts); gait; contour (gross deformity only; subtle malalignment and mild scoliosis aren't relevant); colour (inflammation); scars (surgery the patient forgot to mention).
  • Palpate: of limited value; brief check for tenderness and gross deformity.
  • Movement: flexion and extension, noting reproduction of the typical pain and the rhythm of movement (must match the history; if not, revisit the history).
  • Prone passive extension ("sloppy push-up"), up to 10, when flexion hurts: lie prone, hands palm-down above the head; press the upper body up with the arms until the elbows lock while the front of the pelvis stays on the table; let the low back sag; lower slowly; don't hold. Stiffer spines need the hands further forward. Ask about pain before and after: better, worse or the same. Done prone rather than standing to remove gravity's compression and muscle guarding.

Nerve root irritation tests

TestTechniquePositive
Straight leg raise (L5/S1)Supine; the other hip and knee fully flexed (rotates the pelvis, removing hamstring tightness); examiner passively lifts the straight painful legReproduces or worsens the patient's typical leg-dominant pain, at any angle. Back pain alone is not positive (just mechanical pain). A back-dominant patient shouldn't have a positive SLR
Femoral nerve stretch (L3/4)Passive; patient prone with the knee of the painful leg extended; the examiner lifts the leg into hip extension (student guide). The tutor demonstrated a knee-flexed variantReproduces the typical anterior thigh pain (back pain is common but irrelevant)

Nerve root function (first test in each group = basic screen)

RootTests
L3, L4Knee reflex (seated, leg hanging free); quadriceps power (extend the knee against resistance)
L5Extensor hallucis longus (seated, foot on floor, lift the big toe against resistance); heel walking, 5 steps (+L4); ankle dorsiflexion (+L4); hip abduction via Trendelenburg (stand on one leg; examiner behind with hands on the iliac crests; the contralateral crest drops if the stance-side abductors are weak)
S1Flexor hallucis longus (curl the big toe against resistance); toe walking, 5 steps; repeated toe raises (10 on both feet, then each side, affected side first; examiner steadies); ankle reflex (kneeling); gluteus maximus tone (prone; palpate while the patient clenches 5–10 times: abnormal = tone decreases on the affected side)
Sensation (optional, to confirm level)Pinprick: L4 medial leg/ankle, L5 big toe, S1 lateral foot

Mandatory: upper motor neuron and sacral tests

  • Any UMN finding negates a mechanical low back diagnosis (think cord or brain; refer to neurology): spasticity (velocity-dependent increase in tone); extensor plantar response (stroke the lateral sole and across the ball of the foot: normal is toe flexion or nothing; fanning/extension of the big toe is abnormal after infancy); ankle clonus (brisk dorsiflexion: sustained rhythmic beats; 1–2 beats is normal).
  • Saddle sensation (S2–S4): the same roots supply the sphincters, rectum and bladder; test light touch in the midline between the upper buttocks (prone). If history or exam suggests cauda equina, do a DRE for resting tone and voluntary squeeze ("bear down").
  • Ancillary when the history suggests: hip exam (typical pain on flexion/internal rotation), peripheral pulses (vascular claudication), abdominal exam.

The four patterns

PatternHistoryExamAnatomic correlate (conceptual)
1Back-dominant; always worse with flexion; constant or intermittent (the only pattern that can be either)Location matches; flexion reproduces the pain; neuro normal or unrelated (e.g. an old Achilles rupture)Discogenic (posterior disc bulge on flexion). Disc degeneration ("wear and tear") is part of normal ageing, with genetic, nutritional and mechanical causes
  1 PEPProne extension positive: pain reduced within 10 prone press-ups; a clear directional preference; responds fast with minimal intervention"Simple" bulge
  1 PENProne extension negative: pain unchanged or worse within 10; no directional preference; needs more care and time"Stubborn" or lateral bulge, or too acute
2Back-dominant; never worse with flexion; worse with extension (standing, walking, overhead work); always intermittent. UncommonExtension reproduces the pain; flexion doesn't hurt or helps; neuro normal/unrelatedFacet joints (gymnasts, overhead workers)
3Leg-dominant, always constant; leg pain affected by back movement or position. The only true "sciatica", and even that is a misnomer: the problem is irritation of a nerve root, not the sciatic nerve, and most leg pain from the back is referred, not radicular (so avoid the word)Location matches; must have an abnormal neurological finding: a positive irritative test (SLR/femoral stretch) and/or focal deficitAcute nerve root irritation (e.g. disc herniation); hardest to treat, slowest recovery
4Leg-dominant, always intermittent——
  4 FAFlexion-aggravated (unusual): intermittent leg pain worse with flexion; may have a positive irritative test or deficit; better with unloaded back extensionResidual/adherent nerve root (scarring after old sciatica)
  4 FRFlexion-relieved (common): leg pain brought on by activity in extension (walking, standing) and relieved by rest in flexion (sitting, leaning on a shopping cart); may have transient weakness with activity. Irritative tests negative; deficits only in long-standing casesNeurogenic claudication: transient nerve root ischemia from compression in a narrowed canal and the exiting foramina (spinal stenosis), typically older adults
The decision tree
Back- or leg-dominant? → Back: constant = P1; intermittent and flexion hurts = P1; intermittent and only extension hurts = P2. P1 then splits PEP/PEN by prone extension. → Leg: constant = P3; intermittent = P4, split FA/FR by the effect of flexion. The anatomy is only a guide: a disc bulge can produce P1, P3 or P4-FA. The system is simple to understand but not always easy to apply.

Treatment by pattern

General principles: education (benign and mechanical, often recurrent but controllable; "not the result of a medical condition at all"); counter-irritants (ice, heat, liniment, massage); posture correction; direction-specific movement, prescribed precisely (intervals, reps, sessions per day: "if you don't take it seriously, neither will the patient"). Medication: no narcotics for patterns 1, 2 or 4 (OTC analgesics or NSAIDs with mechanical therapy); acute pattern 3 may need a short narcotic course.

PatternPostureMovement / rest
1 PEPStanding: foot stool. Sitting: large lumbar roll. Lying: night roll; pillow between the knees (upper knee higher than the hip)Unloaded prone passive extensions (elbows locked, hips down, back sagging, slow, not held), frequent sessions through the day; standing extension if effective on exam
1 PENFoot stool; small lumbar roll; night roll; pillow between the kneesScheduled rest in Z-lie or prone over pillows. Progress stepwise: flexion position (Z-lie) → flexion movement (knees to chest) → extension position (prone over pillows) → extension movement (prone press-ups), then manage as PEP
2Pillow between the kneesFlexion: seated slump (shoulders between the knees, push up with hands on knees); step flexion (one foot on a stool, chest to thigh, push up). Frequent; pain control is rapid
3—Scheduled rest: a set time out of every hour in the most relieving position (Z-lie, prone over pillows, prone on elbows, hands and knees); necessary activity the rest of the hour. No exercise while acute. Leg pain settles over 4–8 weeks; back pain then often dominates, so treat as P1. In the rare case where leg pain stays dominant but becomes intermittent, manage as Pattern 4 (the guide prints "Pattern 4 PEP", a typo: read it as 4 FA, which is treated like P1 PEP). Not improving in a reasonable time: consider opioids or decompression surgery (tutor)
4 FAAs P1 PEPProne passive extensions, gentler and over longer; flares managed temporarily as P3
4 FR—Postural control: abdominal/core strengthening, pelvic tilt (student guide); the CBI handout adds sitting flexion and cat/camel and calls a long-term core-strengthening programme the most effective treatment. Gradual improvement, long-term commitment; good surgical candidates (student guide)

Mechanical treatment requires direction and goals based on the pattern; technique is critical and progress is judged by response. If the history fits, the exam fits and a correctly performed programme still fails within a reasonable time, go back to the drawing board (reassess and screen for red flags). Patients under 20 or over 55 still respond, but consider other causes in the young.

The CBI patient handout (small-group practice sheet)

The take-home sheet for the practice session (CBI Health Group; courtesy of Dr Hamilton Hall), one page per pattern. Each item has patient-worded instructions, a photo and blank dosing lines to fill in ("Rest for __ min every __ h"; "Repeat __ times every __ h"; lumbar roll "__-inch"): the guide's "be prescriptive" rule in practice.

PageItemsKey instructions
P1PEP: sloppy push-up. PEN: prone lie (pillows under the hips, or flat), prone on elbows, Z-lie. Both: lumbar roll (sitting), night roll"Start slowly": the first days may be prone lying only, then progress to prone extension with the arms. Push-up: hands beside the head (further up if needed to lock the elbows); pelvis stays down; back muscles relaxed; "Move slowly up. Lock elbows. Sag back. Down." Do not hold. Z-lie: supine, calves on a chair, hips and knees flexed. Night roll: a long sponge roll between hips and ribs so the back doesn't sag
P2Knees to chest; sitting flexion; trunk flexion stretch (on hands and knees, sit back on the heels)Sitting flexion: head and shoulders between the knees, then push up with the hands on the knees; rise using the arms on the thighs. Avoid extension
P3Rest positions only: Z-lie, prone lie, prone on elbows, hands and knees (+ lumbar roll, night roll)Scheduled rest in whichever position most reduces the leg pain. No long-term bed rest. No exercises or repeated movements during the acute attack. Sitting is usually very painful
4 FAThe P1 set: sloppy push-up, lumbar roll, Z-lie, prone on elbows, prone lie, night roll"It is the leg pain that is the focus": a gentle, gradual approach; the rest positions double as the flare plan
4 FRSingle-leg abdominal press, partial sit-up/crunch, sitting flexion, pelvic tilt, cat/camelAbdominal press: hip and knee at 90°, hand presses the knee as the knee pushes back (isometric). Pelvic tilt: tighten the abdominals and flatten the small of the back into the floor. "The most effective treatment is a long-term regular core-strengthening programme"

Handout vs student guide: the direction of treatment matches for every pattern. The handout omits the foot stool, the pillow between the knees, step flexion and roll sizes (guide: large roll for PEP/4 FA, small for PEN), and puts knees-to-chest on the P2 page (in the guide it is PEN progression step 2). For assessments, use the student guide's version.

Three questions: back or leg worst (gluteal fold)? constant or intermittent (completely gone?)? worse bending forward? Plus the mandatory bladder/bowel question. P1 back + flexion (PEP/PEN by 10 prone press-ups); P2 back, extension only, intermittent; P3 constant leg + positive SLR/deficit; P4 intermittent leg: FA or FR (neurogenic claudication). SLR positive only for typical leg pain. UMN sign = not mechanical. Saddle sensation S2–4. Treat by direction: P1 extend, P2 flex, P3 rest positions, P4 FR core and flexion.

Night-Before High-Yield

MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb

Week 38 · MSK II — Rheumatology & Upper Limb
CPC 3 · Year 2
Study Suite
★ Do-not-miss · first-step reflexes
Hot single joint (esp. fever, prosthesis, biologic) → septic until proven otherwise: aspirate (3 C's) + blood cultures before IV antibiotics; drain the joint
GCA (≥50, headache, jaw claudication, vision) → prednisone 1 mg/kg now; visual loss → 1 g IV methylprednisolone; don't wait for biopsy
Lupus flare → creatinine + urinalysis first (GN has no exam sign)
Palpable purpura / sick multisystem patient → think vasculitis, check urine
Methotrexate is WEEKLY + folate daily except MTX day; teratogenic
Before a biologic → screen TB (CXR) + hepatitis B; no live vaccines
Back pain + bladder/bowel change or saddle numbness → cauda equina, surgical emergency

Approach PW01–02

Steps joint? → how many? → inflamed? → clues (EAM)
